speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MESSAGES FROM AND TO THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the house I am sure will be happy to hear the gracious message received from Her Majesty by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday afternoon. The Prime Minister wired her subsequent to her departure in the following words:
As Your Majesty and Prince Philip leave Ottawa to visit the United States of America I send you, with humble duty, a message of loyalty and love from all Canadians. During this historic stay Your Majesty has strengthened in us all our pride in Canada and in Canada's Queen. It is with high hope that you will come to us soon again that I bid you au revoir. May God bless Your Majesty and Prince Philip.
And the reply from Her Majesty reads as follows:
The very kind telegram which you sent to me and to my husband reached us as our aircraft took off from Uplands. I deeply appreciate the message of loyalty which it contains. We have both enjoyed to the full our days at Ottawa and keenly look forward to our return. We send our best wishes and thanks to Mrs. Diefenbaker and yourself.

subsubtopic: DISRUPTION OF COMMUNICATIONS OVER PEACE RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of National Defence whether he can tell the house what action his department will take to replace the bridge at Peace river on the Alaska highway which yesterday, unfortunately, fell into the river and so disrupted communications to our northland.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: DISRUPTION OF COMMUNICATIONS OVER PEACE RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon I was advised by the commander of the northwest highway system that the north anchor and the north cable bent of the bridge on the Alaska highway over the Peace river at Taylor flats had moved some six feet during the night of the 15-16 October.
Hon. members will recall that the bridge was built in 1942 by United States army engineers during the construction of the Alaska highway. Traffic across the bridge
was stopped immediately, and we are seeking suitable means to keep it moving by other routes.
The premier of British Columbia with whom I spoke yesterday afternoon offered the use of the new P.G.E. railway bridge. The feasibility of using that bridge is now being looked into. It is some miles upstream from the site and would require the construction of seven or eight miles of new roads and would also require planking; the rails of the railway have not yet been laid across the bridge. There is also a ferry at Clayhurst which is some 10 miles downstream. That is now operated day and night, and we have made arrangements to collect material nearer to the site of the Peace river bridge in the hope that a larger ferry may be operated there immediately. I have also sent Dr. P. L. Pratley, a well-known engineering consultant from Montreal, to carry out an on the site inspection and he is now flying to the Peace river.
I had further word this morning before I came into the house saying that the Peace river bridge is all down from the north abutment to the north pier including north cable bent. The remainder was intact, as at 2200 hours last night, but the north pier and tower may be slightly shifted.

subsubtopic: DISRUPTION OF COMMUNICATIONS OVER PEACE RIVER
speechtext: Thank you.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF HOG CHOLERA AT LEAMINGTON, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to inform the house that an outbreak of hog cholera has occurred, and I think it advisable at this time to make a statement in connection with it so that exaggerated rumours may not be circulated. The statement is as follows.
Hog cholera was identified on October 15 by clinical and post mortem findings on premises at Leamington, Ontario. Forty-five swine were involved. The premises have been placed under quarantine and the hogs were slaughtered on the same date. Payment of compensation to the owner will be made.
The swine were purchased through a community auction sale on September 26. As a precautionary measure the auction premises were placed under quarantine pending a thorough cleaning and disinfection, which has now been accomplished. All recent swine sales from the auction premises and all possible contacts with the herd are being examined for evidence of the disease. No further cases have been identified to the present. Hogs on all premises adjoining the infected farm are being treated with antihog cholera serum as a precautionary measure.
The last outbreak of hog cholera occurred in western Ontario during May to December, 1953. We hope that the prompt action taken to control this outbreak will be successful, and that it will be confined within a very small area.

subtopic: REPORTED OUTBREAK OF HOG CHOLERA AT LEAMINGTON, ONTARIO
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Notice has also been given in this instance. During the past eight months, has the minister or livestock division of his department received complaints respecting the grading of hogs in Alberta by federal government graders? If so, what action was taken with respect to such complaints?

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for his notice in connection with this question. The answer is as follows. The only complaint with respect to the grading of hogs in Alberta received by the department during the past eight months was a resolution passed at the annual meeting of the Alberta Livestock Co-Operative Limited alleging severity and inconsistency in grading and requesting that graders be rotated weekly from plant to plant. The complaint was of a general character containing no specific charges or evidence to support the general charges.
The application of national standards for hog carcasses on a uniform basis is recognized as being of prime importance and regular checks are made to achieve this objective. The rotation of graders between plants has been a recognized part of the program. They are rotated on a monthly basis, and it is not felt that more frequent rotation would add to the efficiency.
The situation was fully explained in a letter dated September 17, 1957, which I addressed to the secretary-treasurer of the Alberta Livestock Co-Operative Limited.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR DELAY IN GRANTING PROPOSED INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) asked me a question dealing with the freight rate application now before the board of transport commissioners. In a supplementary question he said, as reported at page 35 of Hansard:
Is it not true that the 4 per cent of that 10 per cent which was granted on September 24 will become effective unless some steps are taken by the government?

I replied to him yesterday that I was not aware that any award of 4 per cent had been made but that I would make inquiries and answer today. I am glad to assure the hon. member and the house that no award was made on September 24, but simply the hearings before the board were resumed on that date.
The case which is now proceeding before the board of transport commissioners is in continuation of an application made on May 15, 1956, for authority to increase freight rates, with some exceptions, by 15 per cent. On June 18, 1956, the board permitted an interim increase of 7 per cent and later, on December 17, 1956, allowed an 11 per cent increase in lieu of the 7 per cent.
On August 30, 1957, the railways amended their application to seek a further 10 per cent increase instead of the 4 per cent left in abeyance. It is only this matter which is now being heard and which, as I stated yesterday, will not be concluded until all parties are given an adequate opportunity of being heard. Of course I should state, as has been stated previously in this house, that the board of transport commissioners is a court of record, constituted as such by parliament. Its decisions are subject to appeal, as the Railway Act provides, but meanwhile the matter is sub judice.
Yesterday the railways completed their evidence before the board. Starting today those opposing the application will begin to present their evidence and, as I said yesterday, everyone who desires to make a presentation before the board in this case will, of course, be given adequate opportunity to do so.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR DELAY IN GRANTING PROPOSED INCREASE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. Will the minister bring the house up to date as to the progress the board is making in the equalization of freight rates, so that any future increases in freight rates may be applied in an equal and equitable manner instead of the discriminatory manner in which they have been made in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
If hon. members will permit me to say one word on the subject of oral questions before we proceed with orders of the day, I should like to give one or two references which, being put on the record, will make it more convenient for members to find authoritative statements of the practice on this rather difficult subject. At the beginning of each new parliament the Speaker has made a statement on the subject of the latitude allowed in asking oral questions of the ministers or of others.
There is no express provision for these questions but there is a practice which is more or less well defined by decisions of the past. I should like to refer to the Journals of the House of Commons, volume C of 1956 at page 299 and the following pages, where the Speaker of the last house made his own statement and collected the statements of previous Speakers for several parliaments. The principal citation or the important citation from Beauchesne's third edition is citation 297 which I will read inasmuch as it is quite short. I think it summarizes the situation:
297. A certain number of oral questions are permitted in practice by members, without notice, before the orders of the day are called; but these are merely allowed by courtesy in connection with the business of the house or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. They are always brief, no debate being permitted, and the replies are as concise as possible. The minister interrogated may reply at once or may direct that the usual notice be given. Such questions are governed by the same rules of order as questions of which notice has been given.
One further reference is to the Votes and Proceedings for Thursday, January 24, 1957, where a further statement on the subject is given. That may be useful, particularly to the new members of the house, in ascertaining just what is the scope of this practice, in order to save the Speaker the unpleasant necessity of endeavouring to apply these rules which I myself find are a little bit uncertain and a little bit difficult to understand.

amount of item 692 of the said estimates, be granted to Her Majesty on account of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958.
He said: Mr. Chairman, I think I speak for all members of this committee in extending to you in your first appearance in the chair our hearty congratulations and good wishes for a happy and successful discharge of the duties of your very important office. To those of us who knew you and were your associates in the twenty-second parliament it is a pleasure indeed to welcome you back to membership in this chamber. We know you will discharge the duties that have devolved upon you as chairman of the committees of the whole house with equity and good judgment.
Mr. Chairman, this is the first occasion on which this new House of Commons has been called upon to deal with the matter of supply, and as a vote of interim supply is not a matter which is always easily understood, I shall with the indulgence of the members of the committee who have been here in the past, say a brief word on the subject in the hope that it may clarify for

Interim Supply
the newer members of the committee precisely what we are doing at this time. The situation with respect to the vote of interim supply at this new session of the new parliament is more complicated than usual and, if the hon. members will bear with me, I should like to explain it as best I can.
We are asking the committee today to approve a vote of a total sum of $305,222,335.25 as interim supply, and we wish to do that on the basis of retaining to the committee the fullest measure of control over the voting of supply. The estimates of expenditure are normally prepared in the fall of the year and are tabled in the house early in the normal session, let us say the month of January. Then as the session proceeds, because the estimates are already then three or four months past the date on which they were prepared in the departments and reviewed by treasury board, it becomes necessary for the Minister of Finance from time to time on behalf of the government to introduce supplementary estimates, then sometimes later in the year further supplementary estimates and, indeed, on some occasions a second group of further supplementary estimates. The main estimates are introduced normally prior to the commencement of the fiscal year to which they apply; in other words, let us say in a normal session in the month of January, for the fiscal year which will commence on the following April 1.
Before April 1 comes the estimates for the previous year and all its further supplementary estimates, of course, have 'had to be voted; then the government will begin a new fiscal year on April 1, without normally having made any provision for the supply for that ensuing year. Consequently as the voting of supply occupies a good deal of the time of the committee, it is necessary for the government to ask for votes of interim supply to meet the expenses of government until the time comes when the committee has completed its review and has voted all the items in the estimates. Often that is not done until the month of July or August, that is to say the completion of that voting. Consequently it is not unusual for the committee to be asked to vote interim supply in the spring of the year on several different occasions, usually one month at a time. The purpose of confining votes of interim supply to one month at a time is to ensure to the committee the preservation of control over public expenditure, control over the public purse being one of the principal functions of the House of Commons.
This year, as I have said, the situation is somewhat more complicated than usual. Prior

to the dissolution of the twenty-second parliament the former government had, in the ordinary course, introduced the estimates for the year. Then at a later stage of the session it introduced supplementary estimates and later, prior to dissolution, it introduced further supplementary estimates. Two days ago I reintroduced those same estimates on the terms which I stated at that time, and with those introduced another group of estimates which are called further supplementary estimates No. 2. So now the committee has before it four groups of estimates, the main estimates, the supplementary estimates, further supplemenary estimates No. 1 and further supplementary estimates No. 2.
At the earlier session this year, that is to say the last session of the twenty-second parliament, some of those estimates had been passed, the estimates of the Post Office Department and several other items drawn from other places; but those were the only estimates in the main and supplementary estimates which had been approved in full. What the government has been functioning on-both the former government up to June 21 and the new government since that date -was a vote of interim supply which was granted by the twenty-second parliament prior to dissolution.
Actually at the earlier session this year five appropriation bills were passed. The first two related to estimates for the fiscal year which ended March 31 last, and three appropriation bills were passed with respect to the estimates for the current fiscal year 19571958. The first of those appropriation bills provided one month's interim supply, intended to be for the month of April. The second bill provided a vote of six months' interim supply, intending to carry the government through to October 31. There was a third appropriation bill passed which was designed to carry into legislative effect the approval given by the house to those estimates -all the items of the Post Office Department and some of several other departments- which had been finally passed.
It may seem an extraordinary situation that now, after nearly seven months of the fiscal year have passed, we should be asking for a further vote of interim supply before the main estimates have been adopted, but the situation was inevitable in view of the fact that the government, by reason of legislation passed at the spring session of parliament, has been carrying on merely on a vote of interim supply.
It is recognized by the government that control by the House of Commons over public

expenditure is difficult in this situation because of the fact that when this new house is dealing with the vote which it is now being asked to deal with, and when it comes to deal with the whole range of estimates in final form, those amounts provided for in the estimates have been substantially spent already. That is the situation which confronted the new government as well as the new parliament; the programs involved in these estimates are, naturally, substantially advanced already, and the new government, like the new parliament-I emphasize this- lacked a free hand with respect to the programs involved in many of the items.
I mentioned that the votes of the last session of the old parliament earlier this year were intended to provide the government with supply until October 31, the conclusion of the seventh month of the fiscal year, but as it turns out they will not be adequate for this purpose. Unless the house authorizes a further vote of interim supply now there will not be sufficient money available to meet the expenses of government which would normally be payable on October 31. The reason for that arises from the fact that increases in the salaries of the civil servants, the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were brought into effect by a decision of this government as from May 1, and because those increases have been paid in this intervening period there is now not sufficient money to meet the expenditures of government which will normally fall due on October 31.
May I say also-and this may sound very pedantic and didactic to hon. members who have sat in this house previously-that the government meets its bills twice a month, on the 15th and on the last day of each month. We had enough to meet the expenditures which fell due on the 15th, but we now do not have enough to meet the expenditures which will fall due on the 31st of this month.
It is not possible for this government to defer until the end of the month this request for interim supply because, as members of previous parliaments are so well aware, the cheques have to be made up somewhat in advance; they go to distant places and have to be sent out at least several days before the due date of the payment. In addition, the measure which the government is asking the house to approve today must then go to the Senate. It is hoped to have the measure before the Senate when it reconvenes on Tuesday, and that the measure may be quickly given royal assent so the cheques may be made up and sent out in time to reach the recipients by the end of the month.
I wish to say a word about the manner in which the bewildering series of figures and 96698-5
Interim Supply calculations that were read out by you, Mr. Chairman, in the resolution were arrived at. We are asking, broadly speaking, for a sufficient vote to meet the expenses of government until the end of November. Broadly speaking this is one month's vote, but there are some instances, for example in some of the items, which were introduced early in the fiscal year or prior to the commencement of the fiscal year, which relate to programs which have not simply proceeded on an even basis throughout the whole 12 months of the fiscal year. For instance, some items appertaining to construction, which proceeds more rapidly during the months when it is possible to carry on building under fair weather conditions, fall into this category. Then with regard to the third group of estimates, the so-called further supplementary estimates, some of those involve increases in social security payments which came into effect on July 1. Therefore they apply only to nine months of the fiscal year. One month's vote on account of these items would necessarily be one-ninth of the total of those items rather than one-twelfth, which would be the case with regard to those which were intended to have effect from April 1.
Then with regard to the fourth group of estimates which I tabled two days ago-the further supplementary estimates (2)-those were, broadly speaking, intended to have effect for approximately six months of the fiscal year running from October 1. Therefore to provide sums with respect to those items sufficient to meet the expenditures to November 30 it is necessary to ask for one-third of those items.
In general, however, the pattern is a request for one month's vote and one month's vote only. Those items that I have mentioned particularly are exceptional for the reasons I have indicated. In no case, even though a program is completed or virtually completed, is the government asking for a vote of the entire item. Some of the construction items, for instance, have been completed in full but in every case we are reserving at least one-twelfth of the total in order that the house may have full opportunity of debate, discussion and questioning of the government on such items before it is asked to give final approval to them.
We intend to be jealous to preserve the rights of the house with respect to the control of public expenditure. I assure the committee that it is not, by the measure to be introduced today, being asked to give final and complete approval to any item. In this respect I would remind the committee that there were a few items which were finally approved by the old parliament. Those, of

Interim Supply
course, are law today and they will not be reopened. But with respect to all the other items the house is not being asked to give final approval to the total amount involved in any item; and in keeping with the time-honoured practice I assure the committee that the passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to criticize any item of the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and an undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and not curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.
May I now, sir, again ask the indulgence of hon. members who have sat in previous parliaments. I think it is only fair to the newer members of the house to say a word about the somewhat complicated procedure involved today. Speaking from my personal experience of 12 years ago I can say that the procedure followed with regard to a vote of interim supply can be very bewildering to a new member. In saying a word about this, and in saying what I have said today, which I realize may sound very pedantic to hon. members who have sat here before, I am, I hope, fulfilling on this occasion the undertaking that was given in the speech read by Her Majesty three days ago, namely, that her ministers will take steps to make both houses of this parliament more effective in the discharge of their responsibilities to the people of Canada. It is for this reason that I have trespassed upon the patience of the committee today in the hope of assisting the new members to understand precisely what the house is being asked to do.
We are now in committee of supply, which is one of the three committees of the whole house; and if the committee approves the resolution which is now under discussion the committee of supply will report that resolution to the house, at which time the house will be asked to give it two readings and concur in it. Then I shall offer to the house a motion that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means and then, if that motion is adopted, in the committee of ways and means I shall move the adoption of a shorter but somewhat similar resolution to grant to Her Majesty the sums set out in the interim supply bill.
If that resolution is reported back to the house by the committee of ways and means and read the second time and concurred in there, I shall then move for leave to introduce the bill, and if that motion is approved the bill will be read a first and second time and then we shall go into committee of the

whole on the bill. If after having been reviewed by the committee of the whole the bill is then reported back to the house, the house will be asked to give me leave to move third reading of the bill in order that it may be passed today.
I emphasize all those stages in the procedure by way of stressing the importance attached to the voting of supply and the various safeguards that are provided by the rules of the house for assuring to the elected representatives of the people sitting here in the House of Commons the control over the voting of supply.

Mr. Chairman, my first words, too, sir, must be of congratulation to you in your occupancy of the high office of Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees in this House of Commons. I join with the Minister of Finance in felicitating you, and I am sure that because of your previous experience in this house you will fill your office with decorum and dignity.
I must start, too, by expressing my own personal pleasure at again taking part in financial debates in this house. During the last five years I have not spoken very often in this house and when I did speak it was on fisheries matters; but hon. members who were here in the twenty-first parliament will recall that at that time I had a junior post in the ministry as assistant to the minister of finance and took quite an active part in debates at that time. My hon. friend the new Minister of Finance, of course, also had a junior role at that time, since he was assistant to the chief financial critic, the hon. member for Greenwood.
Our roles are now reversed. We have both gained in seniority but now my friend the hon. member for Eglinton is Minister of Finance and my leader has honoured me by asking me to be the first financial critic of the official opposition. The minister, of course, now has the advantage of the very great resources of the Department of Finance behind him and an extremely capable and efficient staff, one which I think is the envy of the world in terms of financial matters; and I hope he makes good use of that staff, better use than he made of it at Mont Tremblant.
I have a very different advantage in my new role. Hon. members may recall the lamentation of the prophet Job, "Oh that mine adversary had written a book". Well, mine adversary has not written a book. After all. writing a book does imply some thought and consideration, forethought, afterthought and study. My adversary has done much more. He has filled many books, many volumes of Hansard with a torrent of words, speeches on

every conceivable subject as he hurled gratuitous advice to every corner of the house and there was no thought, or certainly little thought, and no revision of what he put in those books.
Since I have assumed the post of financial critic I have been studying these old speeches of the Minister of Finance. Hon. members who were here at the time he made them will recall how hard it was to sit and listen to his flood of words. I can assure you it is a much more appalling task to sit in the library and plunge through the jungle of his excess verbiage, his gross hyperbole, his endless repetition as he pontificated and cascaded advice on every subject to the members of this house. However, I am persevering in this task and summarizing these speeches so that as these financial debates unroll I can show the great difference between the policies preached by the hon. member for Eglinton in his role of opposition critic and the policies practised by the hon. member for Eglinton in his new role as Minister of Finance, and I intend to give some examples in this first financial debate, the granting of interim supply.
The minister has made a clear explanation to the house of the purpose of voting interim supply. It is normally just a routine matter and the necessity arises when parliament has not approved the estimates at the beginning of the new fiscal year and current expenditures have to be met. He has pointed out that because of the election we have already voted seven-twelfths of most of the estimates and even more of some items, without prejudice to our right of detailed examination, to cover the period between April 1, 1957 and October 31, 1957. However, let me tell this committee that the present motion for interim supply is certainly not a routine matter. It is without question the most extraordinary motion in this field ever presented to a parliament of Canada.
In the brief time at my disposal since the minister made his announcement yesterday I have been in the library trying to see if there is a precedent for this course, and I could find none back to 1867. The motion was presented in such a fashion that I was unable to find any precedent since confederation. I did, however, find an earlier precedent by another Tory government of 125 years ago, the family compact. Hon. members will recall the committee of grievance led by William Lyon MacKenzie which presented a petition to Queen Victoria protesting that that government did not inform members of the assembly of the purposes for which the money was requested, nor did they give an accurate account of how these moneys were spent 96698-5i
Interim. Supply
after appropriation by the assembly. It was these grievances in part which led to the uprising of 1837 and then to subsequent parliamentary reforms.
It is because of this action that since 1867 we in this parliament of Canada have followed the practice that only the government can initiate the expenditure of public funds, that a detailed account of the purpose for which the money is requested must be submitted to parliament well in advance of the money being voted, and that an independent audit of the expenditure of these funds after appropriation be made by the servant of parliament, the Auditor General of Canada.
In following this accepted constitutional practice of responsible government the Governor General last Tuesday sent us a message signed by his own hand in which he recommended certain estimates for the consideration of this house. Perhaps I should remind hon. members of exactly what was said. The Governor General's message can be found in volume II of Votes and Proceedings in these words:
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons, estimates of sums required for the service of Canada for the year ending on 31st March, 1958, and, in accordance with the provisions of The British North America Act, 1867, the Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons.
However, when the Minister of Finance tabled the estimates in the house he did not stand behind them in the constitutional practice of responsible government. He differed from the message of the Governor General and said the government did not intend to support all the estimates he was then submitting. He did not tell us what items in the books the government was not supporting, despite the Governor General's recommendation to this house, leaving the members of this chamber in the dark as to what items have or have not received the present government's support. In other words we are asked to vote public money blindly just as in the days of the family compact. His justification for this most unusual course is that it would save work and money to table the estimates of the previous government, and he mentioned $20,000 as the cost of printing new estimates.
Apparently parliamentary rights now have a price tag, and $20,000 is too high a price to permit the members of this free parliament to have accurate information before they are asked to vote over $300 million of the taxpayers' money in a single day.
I can assure hon. members, though, that even this figure of $20,000 is sheer poppycock. Everyone in this house will grant that the new government is under absolutely no

Interim Supply
obligation to support any or all of the proposals in the estimates tabled by the previous government. All that is needed is for the minister to submit the old book of estimates with a printed or mimeographed supplement listing by numbers the items he does not propose to put forward or the items he proposes to reduce. He surely must have such a list, and parliament is certainly entitled to this information. The cost of preparing such a mimeographed supplement would not be $20,000 but only a few dollars.
Yesterday, you know, we received our customary lecture or sermon from the Prime Minister on the rights of parliament, and today we find the Minister of Finance brazenly ignoring those rights. He violates the constitutional position of responsible government that the government stands behind all the printed estimates recommended by the Governor General for the consideration of parliament. He affronts the rights of members by blandly telling us that there are unknown items he is not supporting but about which we have no information. What a contrast here between his preaching and his practice.
There is a second criticism I have of the form of these estimates. We who were in earlier parliaments can remember the financial critic of the official opposition of that day, the hon. member for Greenwood, who is now a minister without portfolio, quoting with great support a British chancellor, I think Philip Snowden, to the effect that a chancellor who took one penny more in appropriations than he really needed-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Half a crown.

I am talking about millions of dollars here. One penny or half a crown; I am glad to find the quotation is approximately right, that a chancellor who took one-half crown more in appropriations than he really needed was guilty of barefaced robbery of the taxpayers. Well, that is in effect what we have been asked to do today. The Minister of Finance is asking us to vote one-twelfth of the general estimates which were submitted by the last government, but he admits that there are amounts in these estimates he will not use; so in effect he is mulcting the taxpayers of unnecessary funds, the type of robbery that the hon. member for Greenwood used to deplore.
There is another aspect to this. The Financial Administration Act, which is the key act governing the finances of this parliament, an act which I piloted through this house when I was parliamentary assistant, does provide that within a department money can be transferred from one item, if it is not

used, to another item subject, of course, to the approval of the treasury board. In effect the minister can now, since we are giving blanket approval to these estimates which are not to be used, later transfer these moneys and add them to the amount of the estimates which he is going ahead with, thus inflating the estimates that we are actually assenting to at this time.
I have a third criticism of a different nature. Hon. members will also recall a speech made by the then leader of the Conservative party, Hon. George Drew, in Saskatoon in 1952, when he told his audience that he and his party knew that at least $500 million could be stripped out of the estimates of the then government without affecting in any way the essential services of government. Hon. members will recall that when Mr. Drew returned to this house the minister of finance first and myself secondly implored him to give parliament the details of those $500 million savings he could so readily effect so that we could strip them off the estimates and thus save the taxpayers that money, but he resolutely refused to give any detail. Nevertheless, Tory speakers on every husting in the country thundered away at the fact that they could strip $500 million off these estimates without affecting essential public services.
Well, today is the first opportunity for the new Minister of Finance to convert his preaching into practice. If he was sincere in his claim that $500 million could be stripped out of these estimates-that, is 9 per cent of the gross estimates-then this is the time for him to show it. Instead of asking for one-twelfth of these estimates to cover one whole month, he should be asking for one-twelfth less 9 per cent, one-twelfth less $27 million, and show that he is practising what he was so loudly preaching just some few months ago. Does he do that? Oh, no; he does quite the contrary. Instead of stripping 9 per cent off these estimates we And ourselves confronted with additional estimates, with his entire blessing, totalling an extra $80 million of the taxpayers' money. What a contrast again between his preaching and his practising.
What position does the official opposition take to this most unusual request for interim supply, a request which clearly violates every constitutional principle of this parliament in the voting of money? If we in the official opposition thought this affront to the parliamentary rights by the Minister of Finance was wilfully done, then we would hold up the supply until he had properly supplied this committee with a detailed list of the items which he and his

colleagues were supporting in responsible fashion, as was indicated by the message from the Governor General. However, since he is just a beginner at his new job, we want to be charitable, and so we believe that he did not do it wilfully but did it through sheer ignorance, through failing to do his homework, through failing to take advice from the very competent and capable advisers in his own department. In these circumstances we merely ask that some time during the course of the day he stand up and read to the House of Commons the list of items in this blue book that he does not intend to support, that he is either going to delete or reduce. In that way we members can properly discharge our responsibilities in voting the taxpayers' money for supply.
In addition, I would request him to ask his colleagues in the government to stay in the house today so our members can secure information from them on the various items they are now going to bring forward in this committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like at the outset to join with the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano in extending to you on behalf of this group our sincere congratulations on your appointment as chairman of committees of the whole house and as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons.
I should like also, in my opening remarks, to say that in our view the comments just made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano cannot be regarded as captious criticism but rather that his points are well taken. The only thing that amazes me about the position of the Liberal party is that their members knew on Tuesday of this week that the Minister of Finance was overlooking the constitutional provision regarding the voting of money, yet yesterday the leader of the Liberal party stood in his place in this house and said that no matter what happened they would not at this time vote non-confidence in the government across the way. We have listened to a speech this morning with every word of which I agree, but I suggest it is a speech that raises a serious question with respect to whether the house should repose confidence in the government sitting on the other side of the house.
While the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was speaking I was reminded of the last time we had a Conservative government in Canada. One of the various phrases that will be remembered in relation to that last government are the words "blank cheque". We all
Interim Supply
recall how Mr. Bennett sought from the House of Commons in the early thirties what was known as blank cheque legislation. Well, the Minister of Finance is not asking today for a blank cheque, but he certainly is asking for an inflated cheque. He certainly is asking us to vote today a sum of money which according to his own words of Tuesday, if we are to take them at their face value, is greater than the government intends to spend.
I share to the full the sense of amazement expressed by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano at the action of the government in having the Minister of Finance present a message from His Excellency the Governor General and then say that the government does not necessarily stand by the estimates which have been tabled in the house. I hope that serious consideration will be given by the Minister of Finance to the criticisms he is now receiving from this side of the house. I think the point made by the last speaker toward the conclusion of his remarks is well taken, namely that the Minister of Finance should tell us today, before he asks us to pass this legislation, what are the items in the main, supplementary and other estimates which the government does not intend to support or which it intends to ask the house to reduce. I certainly will not be satisfied with just a general statement which seems to give the impression that the government is out for economy unless the minister backs up that statement with chapter and verse.
I want to support as well the suggestion made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano that the Minister of Finance ask his colleagues in the cabinet to remain in the house so they can answer questions that may be put to them on the various departments. That, I may say to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, will be a refreshing change. We had considerable difficulty in the last parliament in getting the then minister of finance, whose presence we miss in the house, to get his colleagues to remain in the house. He chose rather to pilot through all interim supply and sometimes supplementary estimates as well. The slogan just prior to the 10th of June was that it was time for a change. I hope that we will at least have a change in that practice and that we can get our questions answered not just by a know it all minister of finance but by the ministers in charge of the various departments. If what I have said sounds like "a plague on both your houses", that is what it is intended to be.
There are certain aspects of the resolution, Mr. Chairman, which interest us particularly. I think it is unfortunate that a lengthy resolution of this kind is presented to the committee of supply and read by the chairman with

Interim Supply
most members not having it before them or knowing what it is all about. I suppose there -are half a dozen typewritten copies of the resolution which were placed on the desks of certain members and I am one of the fortunate few to have received one, but there is no reason why I should have it and not those in the back rows. I feel that a way should be found for this resolution to be printed in advance so that all members can have it and see what it is on which we are voting.
As I look over this complicated resolution, which in typescript takes a full, legal size sheet of paper, with seven or eight paragraphs and figures galore, I find certain items omitted. First may I point out that so far as the main estimates are concerned we are being asked to vote one-twelfth of all of them except those, and they are numbered, concerning which previous votes have brought the total amount released to eleven-twelfths or more. I interpose that there is no suggestion that any items are being excepted from the main estimates today because they are the ones the government does not intend to support.
When we get to the supplementary estimates, and particularly to the document entitled "Further Supplementary Estimates (1)", I note that the Minister of Finance is seeking further votes of those estimates only with respect to items 668, 669 and 670. By this motion today he is not seeking any further vote with respect to items 663 to 667 inclusive. I hope he will make an explanation to us today as to why no further vote is being sought with respect to those items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be glad to do that at this very minute if my friend will permit. The reason is very simple. Those items to which my friend makes reference in the further supplementary estimates, No. 1, require no further vote. They are in effect because the item in the appropriation bill actually effected an amendment of the statutes in question. That applies to statutes like the Old Age Pensions Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act and so on.
Sections 10 and 11 of Bill 418.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The appropriation bill has actually effected the amendment of those statutes. Therefore nothing further is required with respect to those items in the further supplementary estimates No. 1. But with regard to the other three my hon. friend has just mentioned and which are included within the scope of the resolution now under discussion, those are not statutory items. I looked into this matter. I asked the same

question as the hon. member has asked: Why was there a difference with respect to those items affecting veterans allowances? The answer I was given was that those are not statutory items, and therefore require this vote today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the answer the minister has given. Perhaps before I reply to it I might put on the record just what it is we are talking about. Items 663 to 667, to which I referred a moment ago, provided for increases in family allowances, old age security, old age assistance, blind persons and disabled persons allowances. But when these items were put through at the session in April they were put through by the supplementary estimates to the extent of two-sevenths in the case of the family allowance dollar increase and by four-ninths in the case of the other increases. The family allowance increase was to take place on September 1. That meant there were seven months left in the fiscal year, so two-sevenths was the provision for it to be continued for two months, September and October.
In the case of old age pension and other increases they were to be effective on July 1, which meant there were nine months left in the fiscal year so that four-ninths made provision for July, August, September and October. In the case of the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Pension Act the provision was from July 1, and again four-ninths was provided, and I would point out that the wording of item 664, for example, is exactly the same as the wording of item 669, to provide, effective on a certain date, that a certain act is amended.
I bow to the wisdom of the officials who have advised the minister but I find it difficult to do so. It looks to me as though if in one case the act was actually amended by what was done with respect to the supplementary estimate, it should have been so in the other case. On the other hand, I put it this way. If it is necessary by a further vote to continue the increase in the case of the war veterans allowance, it would seem to me that it would be necessary to continue the increase in the case of old age pensions, family allowances and so on. But if the minister can assure us that the law officers of the crown are clear on this point that there is no question as to any lapse in the increase, that is fine; but it is fine only as far as it goes. It seems to me that now is the time for the Minister of Finance to tell us what are the government's intentions with respect to these increases in the old age pension and other benefits.
Today we are being asked to approve the general financial program of the previous

government. We are being asked to approve it with secret modifications that we have not yet been told about, but in general we are being asked to approve what the previous government proposed, which included old age pensions of $46 a month, that miserable sum which the Liberals will now admit was part of the reason for their downfall. But during the election campaign the present Prime Minister promised that if he and his party were elected they would call parliament in September, and would deal immediately with the question of the plight of the old age pensioners and see that the amount of the pension was raised in keeping with today's cost of living. The country had considerable difficulty in getting out of the Prime Minister a precise figure as to what the Conservatives would do with regard to old age pensions, but in this house and in other places he used the figure of $60 favourably. In any case, whatever the amount was to be, we were promised a session in September and immediate attention to the plight of our old age pensioners.
Here we are in October, not September. We have the promise in the speech from the throne, and we in this party welcome it wholeheartedly. But despite that fact I was unable to get from the Minister of National Health and Welfare the other day any indication as to when whatever increases are in store would be effective. Now today we are dealing with these estimates, on the basis of which we are determining the moneys that are going to be paid out by this new government in the month of November, and we are still not being told what the old age pensioners are going to get. Is the pension going to be back at $40 by virtue of our not voting on the supplementary estimate, or is it going to be continued at the level of $46, or is it going to be raised to a new figure?
When he spoke yesterday the Prime Minister more or less dared anyone in this house to suggest that parliament should have been called earlier in view of the fact that arrangements had been made for Her Majesty to be here on October 14. Important and historic as was the occasion in the Senate chamber on October 14, I suggest that it would have been even more historic and even more memorable if Her Majesty had been given an opportunity on that occasion to give royal assent in person to a bill increasing old age pensions and other benefits. That is a bill which would have been passed readily by this House of Commons, if this Prime Minister, who said over and over again that he would keep faith with the people of Canada, had kept his promise and called us here in September to deal with this important issue.
I call on the Minister of Finance, in the course of this discussion today, to do what he and
Interim, Supply
his colleagues told the previous government to do time and time again, namely-take the house into his confidence, tell us what his plans are and what they mean by keeping faith. I call on him to tell us what he himself meant when, shortly after he became Minister of Finance, he announced that there would be a budget this fall and that there would be an increase in the old age pension. In fact I hope he will now answer the telegram which I sent to him at that time congratulating him on his announcement and expressing the hope that he would spell out what he meant by an increase in the old age pension. I have before me a copy of the telegram. It was taken note of by certain newspapers but as yet I have not had a reply from the Minister of Finance.

speechtext:
The
constitutional manner-those words perhaps should be put in quotation marks-of the Minister of Finance is somewhat open to question in view of his action this week in presenting the estimates and telling us that he does not necessarily stand behind the recommendation of the Governor General.
I think we should also have a clear-cut statement on the family allowance question, as to whether any changes are planned there. As a matter of fact, if the minister has any memorandum from the law officers or officials with regard to this difference between old age security and family allowances on the one hand and war veterans allowances on the other, I think he should give it to us. Assuming that nothing has to be done with regard to old age security and so on, I point out that the fact that we have before us a proposal to continue war veterans allowances at the rate now in effect for another month means that the fulfillment of the promise to increase the rate to war veterans who are burnt-out pensioners is now being postponed.
One of the bitterest criticisms made by the Tories in the last parliament was that the government of that day had not increased the allowance to single veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Yet we are now being asked to support a motion one section of which continues for another month the rates as put into effect by the late government, which included no increase in the amounts to single veterans.
In my view that is not keeping faith. It may be fine that these things will be done eventually, but in the meantime the senior citizens of this country die at the rate of 5,000 a month and our war veterans pass on steadily. These people who hoped that as a result of the change in government on June 10

Interim Supply
we would have a government that would keep faith, are wondering when these things are going to happen.
Mr. Chairman, I make it crystal clear that we welcome everything of a legislative character that the government has proposed. We want to see these things put into effect. I was glad that yesterday the Prime Minister suggested that there could be an interruption in the debate on the address-and we will agree to it-in order to put through some of this legislation. But this practice should apply not only to cash advances on farm-stored grain; it should apply particularly to these social security measures and to improvements for the war veterans of this country.
I may have something more to say later on this question of superannuated civil servants. Perhaps I might as well do it right now if I still have left any of my 30 minutes. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that, with the Prime Minister absent today, the person immediately to his left is the Minister of Public Works whom we have known so long as the active and aggressive member for Vancouver-Quadra; and I pay my respects to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, now Minister of Public Works, for the support he has given across the years to the demand for an increase in the pensions of retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower and middle brackets. Yet, Mr. Chairman, despite the hope we had that these people who took that position when in opposition would do something about it when in office, the answer that my friend the hon. member for Fort William received from the Minister of Finance the other day was such that I do not know why the hon. member said "thank you".

If the people of Canada voted for a change, let us have more of a change than we have had indicated in the house this week, and particularly let us have it in the field of these social benefits.
I call upon the Minister of Finance to answer the criticisms that have been made today by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, in which I join, concerning the constitutional provisions about government support of estimates placed before the house.
I also call upon him, before he expects us to approve of continuing all the former government's fiscal and expenditure policies for one more month, to tell us precisely what are the government's plans with respect, to old

age pensions, war veterans allowances and these other social security measures. What are the changes the government proposes; when are they coming into effect; and if they are not coming into effect soon, let him tell us why. The Prime Minister promised to call a session in September to do these things but, to the extent that he failed to do so, he has already broken faith with the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, rising for the first time in this chamber I should like to pay a brief but deeply felt tribute. I must confess that whenever I hear a reference to the member for Vancouver-Kingsway, I instinctively still think of Angus Maclnnis, who from 1930 to 1957 I am sure earned respect and affection in all quarters of the house. I think all hon. members will be glad to know that Mr. Maclnnis is enjoying a well-earned retirement in Vancouver, which is that part of the country most richly endowed by nature and climate for good and healthy living.
Mr. Chairman, before the committee grants the interim supply requested by the minister I think we should be satisfied that something is being done about the unemployment situation on the west coast, particularly in the lumber industry. These things in my opinion should be dealt with before they reach crisis proportions. In the lumber industry, upon which British Columbia depends for perhaps 40 per cent of its payrolls, we do have an unemployment crisis developing. The production of logs from the forests of British Columbia is down about 50 per cent from what it was in October of last year. Sawmills are cutting lumber at about 25 per cent below capacity. The same is true in plywood, with layoffs for some mill workers and short time for others. These are people with families to look after. Even in the case of pulp and newsprint there is oversupply, something we have not seen in British Columbia since the end of the war.
Who knows but that this situation may not very well worsen in the winter months ahead unless something effective is done. Now, I appreciate that the government may not accept the necessity of economic planning for full employment, as advocated in this quarter of the committee. However, I think there is one thing they can and should do, and not delay it any further. I refer to the establishment of an embassy and a trade commission in communist China, with the necessary diplomatic recognition. I heard, as we all did, Conservative speakers in the last election campaign say how much this new government would do to expand trade with China. But how can you expand trade if

you are not even willing to go as tar as extending diplomatic recognition? I say it cannot be done.
I do not need to say to this committee that recognition does not imply approval. Of course it does not. No one could approve of the violence and dictatorial methods which have been part of the Chinese revolution, but at the same time I think no one should be surprised that violence and brutality have followed in the wake of such a shattering social upheaval. The fact is, however, that a new China does exist and we have to live with it. One cannot escape the facts of life and, in the atomic age, it would be very dangerous indeed to try to escape the facts of history. The old order in China will certainly never return, whatever new ideas or institutions may be thrown up before the Chinese revolution runs its full course. The moving hand of history writes and, always, moves on, never backwards.
My recollection, Mr. Chairman, is that in the last year, 1956, communist China sold to us about $5 million worth of goods. Canada, on the other hand, sold only $1 million worth to China. So they had a favourable trade credit in Canadian dollars in that year of about $4 million. I think in 1955 the Chinese credit vis-a-vis Canada was $3 million. That is not much in the total trade picture, but I do suggest that a beginning has to be made, particularly having regard to the need for a share in the market of 600 million people for Canadian wheat as well as Canadian lumber.
A beginning has to be made and the question of diplomatic recognition must be faced. My recollection is that Hon. Sidney Smith, when asked about this question by the press, replied that the matter was under study. Well, there are some times when study is a very poor substitute for decision, and this is one of them. The facts are in, and have been in for a long time. This is a time when the necessary first step-the inescapable first step-of recognition should be taken.
I hope this government will not tamely follow the policy of long delays in acting on this question which was adopted by the last government. If they do that, if they tamely follow that policy, the people of Canada will find that they have had a change without a difference. I would ask the new government whether it is not avoidable that Canada should always be bound to the chariot wheels of United States foreign policy. I would remind them that Britain took the lead in this matter some years ago, and that surely there are times when Canada can give a lead which is as much in the interests of 96698-6

our American friends as it is in our own interests. I do not see the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the committee-

Before the supply is voted I would like either the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Acting Prime Minister to indicate clearly to this committee whether they will not, in view of the trade and peace considerations, take the necessary first step in extending diplomatic recognition to communist China. It should not be said that we are leaving the 600 million people of China without any voice or influence from Canada. It should not be said that China has no place to turn in the western world but that its only place to turn is to Soviet Russia. I therefore hope the government, through its appropriate spoke-men, will satisfy the committee as to this question and the trade question, which matters of course are closely related.

Mr. Chairman, I would like first to congratulate you, sir, upon your election to the office of chairman of committees and Deputy Speaker and to express, with others, the confidence we have in you and your ability to handle these very important duties fairly and justly.
I listened very carefully to the statement that was made by the Minister of Finance. I thought he made a very lucid explanation of the reason for the interim supply, perhaps the best I have heard at any time since I have been a member of the house. It certainly did provide for the new members, and perhaps a good many of the older ones who have not yet been fully immersed in financial affairs, the kind of explanation they require to be able to understand the complicated system that is used.
I could not help feeling as the Minister of Finance spoke and gave us his explanation that part of the complication which he had to face when he took over his new office was inherited from the old government. They certainly left things in a mell of a hess, if I can say that, in so far as the estimates were concerned with which we were struggling last spring.
That may perhaps offer some explanation for the items which have been criticized.
I cannot go along with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at all in demanding that at this time the specific details of the government's legislative program be revealed. It is not customary for any government to do that before the bills are brought down. We all wish to know as early as possible how

Interim Supply
much the old age pensioners are going to get. I would like to know that right now, and so would the old age pensioners, but it seems to me the thing to do would be to grant this interim supply measure as quickly as possible so we can have the bills brought here, and then give the government whatever advice and counsel we are capable of giving with regard to those bills. We want to get those bills here quickly, and while many of us would like very much to be the first to draw from the government the details regarding the amounts to be paid and the times when such amounts are to be paid, we quite realize that that is not customary, and we are prepared to do everything we can to facilitate the passing of other business in order to get the bills here as quickly as possible. We are as interested in war veterans and others as are members of the C.C.F. party, and I daresay the government can say the same thing.
There is one criticism that was made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano with which I think we must all agree, and that concerns the unusual nature of the request made to us today regarding interim supply, in the light of the statement made on Tuesday by the Minister of Finance. I cannot help but agree that in my judgment the house would be in a far better position to deal with interim supply if we had in our hands today a list of those items of the old estimates with which the government does not intend to proceed. At the same time it would have been much better for all concerned if copies of this mimeographed statement had been distributed to all hon. members, and I would certainly suggest to the Minister of Finance that if it is possible for him to do so he should hold over this request for interim supply, possibly for one day or even for two or three days, and give us in the meantime a list of those items in the old estimates which are not to be proceeded with.
It is quite true that if one wishes to make exceedingly fine distinctions and criticisms, the present request for one-twelfth of many of the items, one-ninth in certain other cases, and one-third in one or two remaining cases, if we were to take the minister's words spoken on Tuesday as authentic-and I am certainly prepared tc do that-means that today we are actually being asked to vote more than the government intends to spend, and that has been the object of very serious criticism in the past. I believe that in a situation of this kind there is yet time for the government to rectify its possible mistake and bring before us a list of those items with which it does not intend to proceed, and then we should be in a far better position to hurry estimates through.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to join with others who have spoken in expressing good wishes to you for the successful carrying out of your duties as Deputy Speaker of the house, and I have no doubt you will bring your well-known talents in both languages to the execution of your task.
I would like to speak on much the same questions as were touched on by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I think it will be interesting for the committee to consider this matter a little more fully than we have done up to the present time. I would like to emphasize that we are dealing here, as the Minister of Finance has said in what I might describe as his professorial remarks, with the main estimates, the supplementary estimates and the further supplementary estimates (1) and (2), and if one looks at the Journals for Tuesday one finds, with respect to each of these estimates, the traditional message from the Governor General concluding in each case with the formal statement, "The Governor General recommends these estimates to the House of Commons."
Now, we all know that these recommendations are not made spontaneously by His Excellency; they are made, of course, on the advice of his ministers, and it is perfectly obvious that in the recommendations made to the house in these four messages we are being told that the government recommends the estimates to which they refer to the consideration of the house. And we know, Mr. Chairman, that this is the traditional way in which legislation to authorize expenditure is introduced. The reading of these messages was followed by a statement by the Minister of Finance. I will not read the whole of it, but I would like to read the qualifying phrase, which will be found on page 11 of Hansard:
However, this is not to say that the present government will support all of the detailed programs contemplated when those estimates were originally prepared. Rather, such changes as this government proposes to make in the current year programs will he brought to parliament's attention when the individual items affected are being considered by the committee of supply.
It seems perfectly manifest to me, and I am sure to other hon. members of the house, that the government has had several months, in fact, in which to go through these estimates and decide which of them it proposes to support, and I think this committee is entitled to know formally from the Minister of Finance which are the estimates we are being called upon to deal with, and which ones we shall be asked to consider in some modified form.
Mr. Chairman, I notice it is one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock I had just reminded hon. members of the statement the Minister of Finance made after he had tabled the estimates the other day. I drew attention, by reading a brief extract from his remarks, to the fact that he had in effect said that in tabling the estimates he was not proposing that the government would support all of them when the discussion on the estimates took place, and that at that time changes in those estimates would be brought to the attention of the committee.
I think this is indeed an anomalous situation. In one breath the government formally recommends all these estimates to the consideration of the house, and in the next breath the Minister of Finance, one of those responsible for the recommendation, announces that the government does not intend to support its recommendation for which it and it alone is responsible. Coming from someone who has spoken so frequently about the rights and prerogatives of parliament, this statement by the Minister of Finance repudiating responsibility for an action taken by his own government is strange and makes me wonder whether the government's respect for the rights and privileges of parliament has not somewhat diminished since it moved from the opposition benches to those it now occupies. In fact one might be permitted to say, judging from the answers which have been given during the question period since the house opened, that the degree of transformation that has taken place is already manifest, and we find the same sort of answer coming from the ministers today as those which-

The former government
gave.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I have lived more of my life in opposition than I have in government, and I am coming back to the point in the circle from which I started.
According to the statement made by the Minister of Finance the other day the changes which the government proposes to make in the estimates are to be revealed to us only when the individual items are being considered by this committee. I would like hon. members just to consider for a moment the situation which the government is thus creating.
