In the past the government presented the estimates. The minister gave the facts to the committee, questions were asked, the advisability of the expenditure in question was weighed, scrutinized and examined by the committee, and there was available to the minister who was presenting the estimates the permanent staff of his department which provided all the explanations which the minister himself was not able to present unaided. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the minister responsible for the estimate justified it to the satisfaction of at least a majority of the committee.
What is the new technique going to be? An item will be called. The minister, I suppose, is going to tell us that he does not support it or does not support it to its full amount. Whose function is it then going to be to support the recommendation which the government has made?
I would like to draw upon my own experience as an example. I was very much interested in the activities of the Department of Transport, and as hon. members of the committee know transport is a field of government activity in which substantial expenditures have to be made in order to keep abreast of progress in a field in which developments are continually taking place. My own experience while I was minister of the department was the difficulty of finding sufficient funds to provide for the activities which the department wished to undertake. In the experience I had during the making up of two budgets I found the estimates which I submitted to the treasury board always suffered a reduction because it was not possible to satisfy all the needs and, as there were limits on spending, it was necessary that my estimates should be cut down.
The process was a long and complicated one. The estimates, as certainly the older members of this house know, are prepared initially by the officials of each department. They are reviewed by the deputy minister with the minister and his officials, and then they are submitted to the treasury board. The officials of the treasury board go through the estimates with a fine tooth comb and weed out any expenditures that cannot be fully justified or which can be properly or usefully deferred. And then, as the Minister of Finance knows, these estimates which have been gone over at the official level are considered by the treasury board itself. When they have been finally adopted by the treasury board they are embodied in the estimates which are presented to this house.
Under this practice, Mr. Chairman, so far as the main estimates, the supplementary

Interim Supply
estimates and the further supplementary estimates No. 1 are concerned, these went through the process I have just described, and I assume the further supplementary estimates No. 2 have undergone the same rigorous examination. I ask myself what is going to happen when these estimates come before this committee. How is this committee going to know what action the government is going to take? Ordinarily we know when an estimate is submitted that the government stands behind it and is prepared to justify and defend it. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Finance should take us into his confidence. He should tell us what changes are to be made in the estimates. He should tell us, for example, whether the rumour which has received some circulation in the press to the effect that the estimates of the Department of National Defence are to be reduced by $200 million is a fact or whether it is mere rumour and nothing more than fiction. The Minister of Finance should lose no time in telling us exactly what estimates we are going to have to deal with.
I fully understand and appreciate the technical difficulties facing the Minister of Finance in the present circumstances, the main estimates, supplementary estimates and further supplementary estimates not having been voted. Nevertheless I believe the hon. member for Coast-Capilano this morning indicated a method which could very easily have been followed which would not have cost the sum of $20,000, the figure mentioned by the Minister of Finance the other day, but which would have given the members of this committee a complete understanding of what estimates we are being called upon to deal with and the amount of each of them.

Mr. Chairman, after the great constitutional issues that have been raised here the subject I am going to bring up will no doubt appear to some to be very trivial and insignificant, but there are several minor points in connection with the estimates as they affect the constituency of Port Arthur which I would like to refer to the ministers who answer for these departments.
Before I begin discussing that subject in specific terms I would like to mention that Port Arthur and Fort William form an economic and social unit. For the last 22 years they have been represented by a pair of gentlemen from the same political party and now that twain has been sundered. I might mention that colloquially around the lakehead the gentlemen who formed this twain were known as the gold dust twins. Now the one who has gone, of course, like the ship named after him is in very icy, far-off waters.

I would like to assure the hon. member for Fort William that when I ask questions that may affect the constituency of Fort William I am not doing so in an attempt to engage in controversial strife. Rather it is simply because our two constituencies are an economic unit.
In connection with the sum of $250,000 for the Fort William harbour works in the original estimates and a further $300,000 in supplementary estimates No. 2 for harbour improvements in Fort William, the Minister of Public Works has informed me that there has been an extension of the contract for the dredging in the west port turning base. I would like to know how much of the estimate has now been spent for this particular project in the Fort William harbour. I would like him to go further and tell me how much of the estimate of $500,000 for improvements at the Port Arthur harbour has been spent, and whether there is any money left for work to be carried on this winter.
Several years ago I believe an experiment was tried at the lakehead by a contractor by the name of Hacquoil, doing winter work over the ice in developing breakwaters and groynes. Because of the developing unemployment situation at the lakehead, an emergency program could be carried on in either or both harbours which would employ quite a number of men. If any funds are left it would be a wonderful boon to our particular community this winter.
I should like to ask the minister who answers for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation what research has been done in connection with the television satellite program. The Fowler commission recommends that areas with a population of 5,000 or more should be serviced by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with some type of television satellite station. In both spoken and written answers from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation they advise me that they are in touch with events but that they have absolutely no money to go any farther or even to set up an experimental station. I just wonder whether any of the funds that are to be voted in the estimates for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are for this purpose. I might say it is a live issue in all the hinterland along the north shore of lake Superior.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: And elsewhere.

In backing up what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said, I just wish to express appreciation to the Minister of Public Works for keeping the dredging going in Fort William. It was the first time we

were threatened with a lay-off in dredging before the freeze-up, and the minister has come through just like a Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What an insult!

This applies also to the Minister of Finance, because I remember how he started as the shortstop on our baseball team. He was there on the job, and if he does as good a job on the team of which he is now a member I can tell you he will be No. 1. But I am anxious to hear from him today what is to be done with respect to increased pensions for retired civil servants. I have a resolution on the order paper and I shall have something to say when it comes up, but if I can get the answer before then it will make it easier. Thank you.

I want to say a few words on the question of unemployment because it is directly related, of course, to government fiscal policies. It is a matter of major concern to my constituents, because we have had an abnormal amount of unemployment in Kootenay West during the past summer, and conditions are growing, shall I say, darker every day.
I was rather disappointed with the answer given by the Minister of Labour to a question asked by a member on this side of the house with respect to this matter. He suggested that all his officers were being advised to search for all the jobs possible and to do what they could to provide employment for persons who are unemployed at the present time. I think that is rather a superficial approach to the situation, because as I understand it from the officers in my district that is exactly what they did all summer, without much effect. You cannot blame them, because it is going to take more than the harrowing of old fields to find the employment necessary to keep our working force employed at this time. It is going to take a change in government trade policies; it will depend on government trade policies and government attitude to public development at this time.
I am not one who is given to extravagant phrases or overestimating the situation, Mr. Chairman, but I do say in all seriousness that it is one of great concern to many of my constituents. We are faced with an abnormal unemployment situation at the present time for two particular reasons. The first is the problem facing the mining industry owing to the price of metals and the lack of markets. Then there is the problem facing the lumber industry owing to the loss of markets and the low prices prevailing. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that in that respect I can
Interim Supply
speak from somewhat painful personal experience. In addition to the loss of markets to the lumber industry, quite recently we found that all purchasing of cedar poles had been cancelled or discontinued. The same thing applies to fir poles. These products go largely to the United States.
This situation has not existed in my constituency since depression times, Mr. Chairman. Therefore you can understand the concern it is causing these men and the small operators who have been in the habit of making their living from processing of cedar, fir, tamarack and other poles. In addition to that, we recently had all our contracts for fence posts cancelled, and the market for piling is about 10 per cent of normal at the present time. For these reasons there is considerable unemployment in my district, and it will increase very rapidly in the few weeks ahead.
So far as the lumber industry is concerned, this is no doubt caused by the lack of markets on the prairies, occasioned by the economic circumstances of the prairie farmers, by the lessened housing program this year until recently, and the loss of markets in the United States.
With respect to the possible loss of markets for base metals, I do want to bring to the attention of the house the action that has been taken in my constituency, very largely, by the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers, to bring this matter to the attention of the government, of the members of parliament from British Columbia and of the public generally. I might say they have taken a most constructive approach to what I recognize, and we all recognize, as a most difficult problem. I think we are beginning to realize more and more that economic problems between the United States and Canada have been getting more difficult from day to day. The union drafted a very sensible and constructive brief and presented it to the cabinet. The members of the delegation were very pleased indeed that the Prime Minister saw fit, as I understand, to meet them on the front steps of the parliament buildings and show his interest in their proposal. I understand the brief was presented to the cabinet and every consideration was promised by those members of the cabinet who listened to it being read.
Later on the union called a meeting of the British Columbia members of parliament. Members from all parties in British Columbia attended the meeting and discussed this important situation for a whole day. At the

Interim Supply
conclusion of the day's discussion they came to a unanimous decision. In that connection may I quote the following:
Alter hearing national and local union officers present the union's concern and position, the M.P.'s found themselves in agreement to a man on the following public statement which they wired to Prime Minister Diefenbaker:
"As there is serious danger of unemployment in base metal industries because of depressing prices, the following British Columbia M.P.'s urge that the federal government be prepared to take emergency action to keep base metal mines open."
This was signed by all members present. They represented all parties in British Columbia. The union's efforts in this respect have been so constructive and the matter is one of such great concern to the Kootenays particularly and to British Columbia in general that the union has received the support of the Trail city council. At the regular meeting held on July 5 the council expressed approval of this protest and unanimously passed the following resolution:
That your government take whatever action is felt necessary to protect the interests of our mining and smelting industries.
In addition, chambers of commerce throughout British Columbia and other organizations, including quite a number of unions, have expressed their support and approval.
This is a very serious situation so far as the mining industry and the miners of British Columbia are concerned, and we do urge the government to face up to the problem and take courageous action. It may take some strong action on the part of the government to prevent an increase in duties on imports of base metals into the United States. While the situation is, shall I say, somewhat dormant at the present time, there is no question but that the mining interests of the western states are going to do everything possible to get the United States government to increase these duties at the next session of congress.
I want to say a word or two with respect to the lumber industry. That industry can be assisted by the development of markets in Great Britain-there are possibilities there-and by government policies which will improve our markets in Canada. In addition, I think this is the appropriate time for the government to consider a revision of taxation policies in so far as they apply to the forest industry, and that section of that industry which is practising conservation methods.
In the past income taxation policy has been one of dealing with these cases on their merits. Each individual case was dealt with on its merits and, in my opinion, much to the advantage of the large operators. Like other members of this group I believe in a mixed economy. We believe in a diversified

economy, and we know the value of the small businessman, small industries and the small service operator to our economy in maintaining its diversity. I suggest in all seriousness to the Minister of Finance that this is a very appropriate time for a reconsideration of the taxation levied on the lumber industry, and particularly that section of the industry which practises conservation in its operations.
In that respect I should like to quote briefly from an address given to the 1956 British Columbia natural resources conference by D. M. Carey, assistant forester, working plans division, British Columbia forest service. Mind you, this is a government servant speaking, and in his very excellent address he says in part:
Thus many influences tend to squeeze the smaller forest owner and operator out of independent existence. We have heard it said, "The small logger is doomed." This may well be so in that his days of independence are numbered as things stand on the coast. In the interior he may survive for a few years. Before going any further let me say that personal views which follow are my own views as a forester and therefore they are not necessarily the views of either the B.C. government or the forest service.
I do not think anyone wants to see the small logger liquidated. Is it not better to convert him into an independent logging tree farmer rather than into just one of many wholly dependent subsidiaries or employees of large corporations?
It is the responsibility of the provincial government, Mr. Chairman, to deal with provincial taxation and to determine the type of forest tenure that shall exist in British Columbia, but it is the responsibility of the federal government to devise income taxation policies that will promote the conservation of our natural resources, that will deal fairly with those who are willing to protect them and will protect the interests and rights of the smaller loggers, lumbermen, tree farmers and so on. I do ask the minister to review the policy that has been followed in the past and give consideration to the matter at this time. This is an appropriate time in that those in the lumber industry, particularly the smaller operators, are having a most difficult time to survive and in most cases are not receiving any compensation, shall I say, for trying to preserve the forests for future generations.
However, while we may do something by government policy to increase our trade with Great Britain and improve our markets in Canada, and may do something to a limited extent to improve our markets in the United States-I am not certain what we can do in that respect-only so much can be accomplished because we are harrowing old fields. We are intruding into developed fields while at the same time half the world goes hungry

and lacks the ordinary necessities of life required for a civilized existence. If we face this fact fairly and squarely I think we must realize the limited opportunities there are in the fields that are more generally mentioned compared with the opportunities presented to us in the other half of the world that lacks so many things that we enjoy.
In British Columbia both management and labour recognize this fact. As was so well expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway this morning, they have indicated their recognition of this fact and their support for policies meant to improve the marketing situation in this country, to prevent unemployment and at the same time accept some responsibility for the other half of the world which, as I said before, lacks the things we enjoy. Together with other members of this group and industry and labour in British Columbia I do urge the government to face the situation realistically and recognize the government of China. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway said, that is not recognition or support of their policies and principles, but we have got to face facts. In recognizing China we will be able to try to develop trade with China, and trade with China means trade with 600 million people who at present require many of the products that we produce.
I might say in passing that the Conservative candidate who ran against me in the last federal election, a very fine gentleman indeed and a good friend of mine, was most ardent in his support of recognition of China and the development of trade policies with China.
I hope the government will listen to the policies advocated by some of its defeated candidates now that it is in power, and will do what some of these candidates were suggesting it should do.
I mention this particularly, Mr. Chairman, because, as I said before, we can only do certain limited things by harrowing old fields. We have got to broaden out. We have got to find other markets that exist, and accept our responsibilities on a world-wide basis. I urge the government to act boldly, recognize China, develop trade with China and in so doing prevent unemployment in Canada and assist the hungry and underprivileged people of the rest of the world.

speechtext: Far be it from me to interrupt the speech of my hon. friend. I gather that he is fairly well through with it by now, is he not?

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has been in this house for 12 years, but he has always sat on the opposition side. Before too long he will learn that the quickest way for a minister of the crown to gain wide acceptance in this house is to recognize that he is not the only member in parliament.
I want to join with others, Mr. Chairman, in congratulating you upon your designation

as chairman of committees of this house. This is an honourable role which I am sure you will discharge responsibly and prudently.
I have some observations that I wish to address to my successor, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. May I say to him, first of all, what I have said to him privately already. I am sure that every member of this house joins with me in extending to my hon. friend sincere congratulations upon his being designated as Minister of National Health and Welfare. I am sure he will find this department an extremely rewarding one. I hope his tenure is brief, but I hope and believe it will be constructive, as he will bring to his assignment the kind of energy and devotion of purpose which have characterized most of his activities, other than his political activities, throughout his life. I am sure he will find this department to be composed of men and women who are devoted to the public service and to the welfare of this country in the pursuit of matters having to do with health and welfare.
I fully appreciate the fact that one could not expect the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is responsible for the expenditure of a larger sum of money than that expended by any other department of the government other than the Department of National Defence, to have at his finger tips the answer to every conceivable question that might be directed his way. I do not want him for a moment to think I am taking advantage of this situation today. That is not my intention. If there are questions that I put to him the answers to which my hon. friend has not at his finger tips at the moment, I am sure we would all readily understand the reason. But I believe this particular question is of such a nature that at least my hon. friend would be expected to have the answers, as I am sure he has because they are of a general character.
I refer, of course, to the matter I raised when the house met on Tuesday last. I asked the Prime Minister whether any significance was to be drawn from the fact that in the speech from the throne delivered by Her Majesty no reference had been made to the matter of hospital insurance. I asked whether any significance was to be drawn from that omission, and the Prime Minister said that I would be unwarranted in drawing that conclusion. I therefore take it that the policy of the present administration is to do everything it can to bring about an implementation of the system of hospital insurance and diagnostic services which was proposed by the previous government and supported by every member of this house. But as we have not had much indication-if I may say so 
with great respect-of interest and have had little indication of detail, one wonders whether or not the government is vigorously pursuing the possibility of reaching at an early date some agreement among the six consenting provinces and others in respect of the matter of hospital insurance.
The other day, in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, my hon. friend said that six provinces had accepted in principle the proposals made by the federal government in this matter. My hon. friend will not misunderstand me when I say that information was not new. That information was available to the people of Canada before the election on June 10 last. The fact is that before the election took place six provinces had agreed to the proposal put forward by the federal government under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Those six provinces had been named exactly in the manner and in the order which my hon. friend himself used the other day; that is to say, the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island had accepted the proposal put forward by the federal government.
One would want now to inquire what situation has developed since the announcement of the consent by these six provinces. Have any agreements been signed? If no agreements have been signed, when is it expected that agreements will be signed? What negotiations are now under way which could result in signatures by provinces of agreements put forward by the federal government or mutually devised or conceived by the federal government and the provincial governments? Has any master agreement been prepared?
The situation prevailing before the previous government went out of office was this. We had discussed with the province of Ontario the terms of a master agreement by which we hoped to be able to conclude the positions taken under the hospital insurance act and provincial enabling legislation. Has the work which resulted in the last conference between the federal government and Ontario been expanded, or has it been decided not to have agreements, as was proposed by at least one of the provinces? What is the situation with regard to the province of New Brunswick, the province of British Columbia and the province of Nova Scotia?
I had been informed, and I so announced in the house, that the premier of the province of Nova Scotia had indicated that he thought this was a measure deserving of support by that province. He told me that there were still some problems which were

concerning him, and I have since learned from the press that he has established some sort of commission to re-examine the whole problem in the light of Nova Scotia's special interest. In this connection it should be noted, of course, that the previous administration in Nova Scotia had set up a commission of inquiry, and that commission had come to the conclusion that it was in Nova Scotia's interest to accept the federal proposal.
Is the minister in a position to tell us whether or not he has reasons to believe that there will be some considerable delay on the part of Nova Scotia in accepting the federal proposal? I had been told some time at the end of May by the minister of health in New Brunswick, in the presence of the minister of health of Nova Scotia, that there was no doubt that the province of New Brunswick was going to come into the scheme and that we might look forward to ready acceptance at a fairly early date by that province of the proposal put forward by the federal government.
These questions are not idle questions, because this whole matter is an important one. The previous government did not arrive at the decision to put forward a proposal which involves very considerable expenditure of public funds without the gravest consideration. It followed as the result of careful consideration by the executive arms of government, both federally and provincially. It was the result and the product of many conferences between the federal and provincial governments. There can be no mistaking the fact that there is a wide acceptance throughout Canada of the desirability of having hospital insurance, and it would be nothing short of a calamity if any undue delay in this matter was deliberate on the part of the present government. I am not suggesting that it is-

Few took a more active part in the deliberations than the Minister of Finance who now looks on and listens to what I am saying, apparently with such great and understandable interest. Notwithstanding that, we have had very little mention at all about this question of hospital insurance by the present administration. With the sole exception of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I am not aware of anyone on the other side saying anything by way of support of this measure, except

when the Prime Minister himself, speaking in Winnipeg, made reference to what he thought were some weaknesses of the project. Since the election, however, no one has made any reference to the matter of hospital insurance, certainly not a minister other than the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I commend him for the words he used when he recently took over the administration of his department. He said that this was one question that was going to engage his full attention, one matter to which he was personally greatly dedicated. Outside of this observation we have heard nothing from any of his colleagues, before or after the election, and since the election, so far as I am aware, nothing whatsoever from the minister himself.
Now, we are surely entitled to know whether any progress at all has been made in this matter. The province of Ontario has indicated that it proposes to implement its scheme on January 1, 1959, and when I last conferred with them in my own capacity as Minister of National Health and Welfare I was informed by the premier of Ontario that not later than the end of September he should be in a position to know definitely whether or not the federal government would be able, pursuant to the act, to provide the government of the province of Ontario with its share of the cost of the operation of the Ontario scheme.
Unless some progress has been made I am afraid this situation is not calculated to give much encouragement. If Ontario is going to begin its scheme on January 1, 1959, unless it is to bear the full cost itself it must immediately know whether the other five consenting provinces will have conformed to the requirements of the hospital insurance act, since that legislation provides that the federal money shall be paid only when the six consenting provinces have schemes in being and in support of which the proclamation of the measures under which they operate has taken place. In other words their legislation must be in force and their scheme must be in force. That certainly is not the case in any province except the provinces of British Columbia and Saskatchewan.
What is the situation in Alberta? Does the minister regard the existence of what they have in that province now as sufficient to comply with the act? What about the province of Newfoundland? Does the existing scheme there satisfy his requirements or the requirements as envisaged by the law officers of the crown? What about Prince Edward Island?
If no agreements have been signed, well then, it is clear that Ontario's position, in

so far as the starting date announced by the premier is concerned, is in great jeopardy unless the minister is prepared at some later date to suggest to this committee that there should be an amendment to the act to provide for payments on a basis not now envisaged by the hospital insurance act itself.
In the province of Ontario there is a demand now being made, and an understandable demand, by the insurance companies and by those who are beneficiaries or who are insured under private hospital insurance schemes, for information on the kind of rates that are going to be imposed under the scheme to be brought about at some future date by the government of Ontario. The trade unions and employers of labour are also very interested in knowing what are to be the rates under the hospital insurance scheme in the province of Ontario and, as my hon. friend knows and as I know very well, there are literally thousands of groups all over the country-I mentioned Ontario particularly since that is the province where the greatest job has got to be done because of the numbers to be covered-who are all awaiting very anxiously to know what will be the situation in that particular as well as in other particulars.
What is the real situation? Are any negotiations under way between the federal government and any one of the provinces? Are there any negotiations under way right now between the province of Manitoba and the federal government? The premier of that province is reported as saying that Manitoba is just as good as in. What is the situation in that province? Perhaps the Minister of Finance, either today or on some later occasion soon, will be able to give us some indication. Has an agreement been signed with Saskatchewan? There should be no delay there now because they have a scheme in being; they were prepared to accept the basic proposals embodied in the main agreement that we had worked out in a general way with the province of Ontario. Surely there should be some agreement signed between that province and the federal government. Has any agreement been signed with any province? If no agreement has been signed, what exactly is the situation?
The present Minister of Finance will recall that his party took a strong position in the matter of certain exclusions. The minister moved an amendment in this house to the effect that tuberculosis and mental illness should be provided for in some form. We maintained that as the act was designed to help individuals and not to subsidize provincial governments, as long as provincial governments continued to bear, substantially,

the cost of the care of those two illnesses, that should not be a continuing charge on the federal exchequer. But that was not the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. You voted against it.

My hon. friend is going to speak later, and I welcome it. Notwithstanding that, he took the position that those two forms of illness should be included and covered under the hospital insurance act. What is the position of the government now? Does it intend to include tuberculosis and mental illness? I am not arguing whether or not this should be done at this time; I am simply wanting to inquire. Is that one of the reasons why the government is not proceeding with the measure? I am told on fairly reliable authority that the Minister of Finance, whose generosity knew no limits when he was sitting on this side of the house, said to his colleagues, "We certainly cannot do all the things that we promised; there is not enough money".

speechtext: Oh, such rot.

My hon. friend says "such rot". It is certainly the kind of rot given out during the election, because there was no limit to what was promised. But I am told the Minister of Finance has taken that position, and he can deny it if he wishes.

What is the position? Are tuberculosis and mental illness to be included in the deal with two of the provinces. One of them, in the maritime area, is prepared to go in right away if the government will live up to the position it took when it sat in opposition. I do not know whether or not that is the case, but surely we ought to be informed about this measure by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speechtext: Will the hon. member for Essex East permit a question? He will feel it is quite natural to receive a question from me. Would his party now support legislation to extend this coverage?

The hon. member may on occasion find it would be possible, sitting in that eternal position of opposition as he does, but I am expressing my personal view. As long as the provinces continue to bear the substantial responsibility for the

care provided to their citizens in the matter of tuberculosis and mental illness, then the hospital insurance act should not be used to subsidize provincial governments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then you have been asking the government to do something that you are not prepared to do.

No, I don't think the hon. member is fair. I am not asking the government to do something I am not prepared to do myself. I am trying to ascertain if despite the position taken by the government when it was in opposition they are now prepared to oppose that position, that opposition being, I am told, one of the reasons why at least one province is not coming in. That is surely a consistent and honourable position for me to take. But if the provinces and the federal government are able to agree on the assumption of this responsibility under the hospital insurance act, then I would have no quarrel, and then it would be the responsibility of hon. gentlemen opposite who have close and influential connections with provincial governments to see that those governments do something, for instance, by way of paying adequate supplementary old age pensions in their respective provinces with the money thus saved.
What is going to be done about depreciation? Hon. gentlemen opposite argued that we were at fault in not including depreciation in the shareable cost. Is that still the position of the government? Is the Minister of Finance now prepared to say through his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or on his own assertion, that the government is now willing to include this additional item? The Minister of Finance says nothing on this subject. He says nothing on whether or not they are going to include tuberculosis and mental illness, and his silence on these matters, as well as the silence of all others in respect of this particular situation, is responsible for the feeling that now exists in all parts of Canada that this government is going to find a convenient way out of doing anything about the matter of hospital insurance so far as the federal government is concerned.
If that is not the situation, why was it not mentioned in the speech from the throne, and why have we not been informed in this house, or before we met, of the progress that was being made? Why have we not got agreement with the provinces in respect of a matter which was brought before this house and which was referred to by the present Prime Minister as the most important social act ever presented to this parliament

If this is an important matter, then the Minister of Finance should, not tomorrow but right now, give an answer to what I have asked and take the opportunity of saying when we may expect action on the part of the government in respect of this vitally important matter.

I will have something to say about what I think was the only point my hon. friend made during the course of his remarks. I will come back and deal with the first one which I thought was his real point, but let us now have a look at what he said were his second and third points.
Concerning the measure before the house today he said his second criticism was on the ground of the form of the measure. It simply follows the time honoured form. Somehow or other the hon. gentleman led himself on from that assertion to say the government was mulcting the taxpayer of unnecessary funds. That was a remark made about the estimates which he and his colleagues drew and introduced in this house last spring, and if there is any mulcting of the taxpayer of unnecessary funds the responsibility lies and will continue to rest on him and his colleagues.
I simply make this observation in passing, that no item is being passed finally today. If the measure the government has introduced passes there is no final decision on any item.
The hon. gentleman has been out of touch with finance, as he revealed today, much too long notwithstanding his experience at one time as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. He undertook to tell the committee that there was power on the part of the government once these items were voted to transfer moneys back and forth. He ought to know and surely I should not have to remind the hon. gentleman after he has been in the house for 17 years that it is not possible to transfer money from one item to another.
Within a department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not within a department. It is not possible to transfer moneys from one item to another. The items are statutory when they are passed and all that can be done is transfer amounts within the details of an item. No money can be transferred from one item to another and it is high time the hon. gentleman learned that if he is going to discharge his new function.
And then in dealing with what he called his third point the hon. gentleman went back to Saskatoon in 1953.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member got his
tenses all mixed up; one minute he was out in Saskatoon and another minute he was in Ottawa; one minute dealing with 1953 and the next minute back dealing with 1957. To my very great surprise indeed the hon. gentleman complained that parliament had not been called in September. It is well that we should pause for a moment to consider
