the significance of what the hon. member has said and the fact that on this complaint he built a baseless assertion that the Prime Minister of this country has broken faith with the promises made in the election campaign.
What was the fact, sir? When we came into office we found that the previous government had already long before committed the use of these buildings to an international conference. We did not have the details of the sittings of that body, but the fact is that the meetings of that international postal conference did not end in this chamber until October 3. What was much more significant, as the Prime Minister explained yesterday, was that the plans made for the visit of Her Majesty had been substantially advanced.
By a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say that had the incoming government not proceeded in the light of the plans that had already been made and invited Her Majesty to open parliament, such a loss would have fallen on the Canadian people that no amount of talk on the part of my hon. friend until doomsday would ever repair; for something has been given to the soul of the Canadian people this week by the visit of Her Majesty and Her Majesty's opening of the Canadian parliament that will enrich that soul for generations to come.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Your speech will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend then went on to say that he wanted to know what was to be the basis of the new pensions that the government is proposing in the throne speech, and he wanted those included in the scope of the present measure. For one who is supposed to know something about the rules of the house, did you ever hear anything more utterly outlandish, did you ever hear of anything as unconstitutional? We are not including in the scope of the measure today payments for measures that have not even been introduced in the house, let alone brought here with a recommendation of His Excellency. Are we to be told now by the hon. member that we should be making disclosures here and now of the intent of the government with respect to the contents of legislation long before the resolutions, which must have the approval of His Excellency, are introduced in the house? I was surprised beyond measure to hear doctrine like that coming from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I can assure him that it is the intention of the government to follow strictly constitutional practice in this matter, and those measures that I think all hon. members, those on this side of the house as well as those

Interim Supply
on the other side of the house, are awaiting with no little interest will be introduced in this house just as quickly as the transaction of business in the house will permit. That means the completion of the speech from the throne debate and the emergency measure with respect to cash advances on farm-stored grain. We hope then to get on with all dispatch with these measures respecting increases in social security benefits and I hope we shall have my hon. friend's support in trying to expedite the program.
I may say to him when he complains that I did not answer a certain telegram he sent me back in the summer that I would have been violating my constitutional duty as a minister of the crown to have informed him of the contents of whatever it might be that the government intended to bring in later on by way of a measure, and that, from an hon. gentleman who has devoted long years to the assiduous study of the rules of the house.
Now, sir, he has asked for some further assurance in regard to these items in the further supplementary estimates, No. 1.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I will have to ask my hon. friend to wait until the conclusion of my thirty minutes. My time is limited. I will be glad to deal with all questions if he will permit me to conclude my remarks. I am a little concerned about the time.
My hon. friend wanted some further assurance about the position of the items in the further supplementary estimates, No. 1. There were eight of those items and five of them were carried into effect by the form of legislation that was contained in the appropriation bill. Those are statutory items and I am assured by the law officer of my department that no further vote is necessary in that respect. Those payments are provided for fully for the remainder of the current fiscal year to March 31 next.
But the three final items, which are the ones referred to in the sheet which I sent him, have not attained statutory effect as a result of the appropriation bill which was passed. It may be that they were intended to have that effect, but I am informed by the law officer of my department it is necessary to make a special provision in the present bill in order to continue payment of those items, and I hope we shall have the support of the committee in seeking to do so.
Sir, I wish to come now to what my hon. friend from Coast-Capilano had to say, echoed as it was by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount. Let me say to the committee that the government is today not only following the constitutional course, it

is following the only course that was physically open to it in the circumstances. It was a physical impossibility to rewrite the whole volume of estimates in the time available. The work that has been indicated with respect to seeking to find savings, where savings could be made, in the volume of estimates that has been re-introduced in the house, is a continuing task and it is going to be carried on.
The committee today is not being asked to overvote any sum, and we stand as a government behind every item for whic'h we are asking today; that is to say, to the extent to which we are asking for it. We are standing back of it and it is perfectly clear and was made perfectly clear this morning.
What is the great to-do that was made by hon. members opposite? What is the substance of it all?
There are 802 items in these four groups of estimates altogether. In the main estimates there were 537 items. Four of them were finally adopted by the former parliament; 533 remain. Of these 533, there are 15 on account of which we are not asking any further vote today; on 10 we are asking for a little more than one-twelfth; on the remaining 508 we are simply asking for one-twelfth, the equivalent of a month, and that does not carry them beyond their proportion of seven-twelfths. There is therefore ample room to do all that the government may wish to do by way of saving without trespassing one inch upon the prerogatives, the duties and responsibilities of parliament.
Of the supplementary estimates there were 47 items. One was finally voted by the former parliament; 46 remain. On two of these we are not asking for anything further. On the other 44 we are asking for only one-twelfth, the equivalent of one month. Of the further supplementary estimates No. 1 there were eight items. Of these five were finally voted by the former parliament and three remain. On these three we are asking simply for one-twelfth, the equivalent of one month.
Of the further supplementary estimates, No. 2, I should note that it was clear to hon. members opposite that the government, having introduced these, is standing behind them all 100 per cent. But if hon. members opposite are still querulous on that subject, let me say to them that of the 110 items therein, on 107 of them we are asking simply for one-twelfth, the equivalent of one month's vote. That means that out of 802 items there are only 13 of which we are asking for more than one-twelfth, and with respect to every one of those 13 there is an explanation which I shall be happy to give and which I know

will satisfy the committee and even hon. gentlemen opposite because I miss my guess if they are prepared to challenge what we are asking for in any of these. I shall be glad to give full details of these. There is a special reason in every case and a satisfactory reason.
I repeat the undertaking that I gave this morning and which in the 12 years that I have been in this house has been given by ministers of finance on every request for a vote of interim supply, I suppose 50 times in those 12 years, that the passing of this bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply. The usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said this morning that there was no precedent for what is being done here, a government submitting to the house a message from His Excellency recommending certain estimates to the house and then not being prepared to stand behind them. Precedents, he says! Well, sir, what are the facts? I wish there were time, Mr. Chairman, but I have time only to give the house 13 precedents on the subject. I have not gone back of the fiscal year 1940-41-
That is an unlucky number.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -but there is a series of items in estimates from that time down to the past session where items were introduced by the government in the form of a message from His Excellency recommending them to the consideration of the house and ministers of the last government when those estimates were reached, in many cases after portions of them had been voted by way of votes of interim supply, rose and withdrew them or submitted to reductions in them.
That is not a precedent at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not quarrel with their reduction or withdrawal of those items. I believe that they should have withdrawn or reduced a great many of the items they tried to stuff down the throats of members of the last three parliaments.
But where is this great principle? We were told there is precedent for such a thing! I well recall an experience of my own when Mr. Winters was minister of public works. You will find it recorded at page 4263 of Hansard of April 29, 1954. An item was called of something over $1 million. I asked some questions about it and it turned out
Interim Supply
that there was a whole lot of money in that item that was not required. What happened? The government of that time did not even wait for me to move a reduction. The gentleman who two months later became minister of finance rose and moved the reduction in that item, an item that had come to the house with the approval of the governor in council.
Was there any shrieking then about the violation of some constitutional principle? Oh, no! It just depends whose ox is gored. But I will be glad to give chapter and verse for what I have said in regard to all of these items of estimates in the years from 1940 to 1957. In the fiscal year 1940-41 there was item 38; in 1941-42 item 137; in 1942-43 item 200; in 1949-50 item 607, in 1951-52 item 650; in 1953-54 item 487; in 1954-55 item 535; in 1955-56 items 331 and 544; and in 1956-57 items 386 and 289.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When I have completed my remarks I will be glad to have any questions that hon. gentlemen wish to ask. I made that clear already.
Now, Mr. Chairman, because we are subject to a time limit I hope that hon. gentlemen opposite will have the goodness and the responsibility to come back and ask me with regard to these 13 items for the reason why in every case it is necessary to ask the house to vote more than one-twelfth. I remind the house, as I said this morning, that in no case is the total vote being exhausted. There is still ample room for the exercise of the responsibility of every member of the house. There is at the same time ample room for the efforts that the government is assiduously making to achieve savings in the interests of the taxpayers and of sound government.
But let me say this in the several minutes that remain to me. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano spoke in a loud voice today and with great assurance until he came near the end of his remarks. But then we witnessed what we witnessed yesterday in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, a bold start, a strong middle part of the speech and then in the conclusion a sad faltering.
If this government is guilty of what the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said about it this morning, then it is perfectly clear that as a government we have no right to sit in these places. We ought to be discharged from office if we have violated the decencies of the constitution and the rights of parliament as he asserted today. But by the same token, having regard to the responsibilities

Interim Supply
of an opposition and, above all, an official opposition and, above all, that of the spokesman on financial matters-
Watch your temper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -for that official opposition, what have you to say, sir, about the sense of responsibility of a spokesman for the opposition who in a matter of that kind accuses the government of violating the rights of parliament and constitutional decencies and then stops short of being prepared to challenge the right of the government to retain office? I say that that weak-kneed course of action is a demonstration of irresponsibility, and I warn hon. gentlemen opposite that if they think that they can deliver these sniping speeches, deliver themselves of these hit-and-run efforts and not be called to account in the house, they are mistaken.
Don't threaten.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After what was said this morning I can assure them that they will have full opportunity to declare whether they have confidence in the government or whether this government is no longer to retain office, for it is my intention-I make it quite clear now-to press for a division on every stage of this measure today in this committee, in the committees that follow and in the house. Personally I am going to watch with the closest interest the vote that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano casts. I shall be asking myself how he is going to cast his vote. In the first place, is he going to vote?
He will vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is one question. Question No. 2: If he is going to vote, is he going to vote in the vein in which he spoke for the first 90 per cent of his speech today or is he going to turn tail on his speech and run?
I am sure there is no question in hon. members' minds who has delivered the louder speech today.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Or who has delivered the best speech.

Now that the sound and fury have temporarily subsided, I want to return to my original point. When I spoke this morning I drew the attention of the committee to the remarks that the minister made on Tuesday, October 15, though not in quite the same loud voice, remarks unique in the history of this parliament. The so-called precedents he has now recounted to us are not,
[Mr. Fleming.!
as I will point out in a moment, precedents at all. But this is what he said, as found at page 11 of Hansard for last Tuesday:
However, this is not to say that the present government will support all of the detailed programs contemplated when those estimates were originally prepared. Rather, such changes as this government proposes to make in the current year programs will be brought to parliament's attention when the individual items affected are being considered by the committee of supply.
All we asked this morning was that the minister tell the committee what items he is supporting in accord with the governor general's recommendation and what are the items which, as mentioned here, he has not committed himself to support. That is what I asked the hon. gentleman, and in the midst of all this crescendo of sound coming from this little man there was one thing he said: We stand behind every one of these estimates presented this day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.
That is exactly what we asked him to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Those are the very words, the very words-
Behind the bill.
-and I thank him for that assurance because now he is showing more good sense than he has showed so far-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are running out.

-in his conduct of affairs as Minister of Finance. Let me tell you about these estimates he is standing behind. These estimates, concerning which he has been unable to give us one single item that he will not approve, were prepared by the gentlemen who now sit on this side of the house, and naturally we are going to support every single item of these estimates that we prepared.
We are not turning our backs on our own work. What we wanted from the minister was some indication of those items for which he was not taking paternity. He has apparently taken paternity for all these estimates. He went to some trouble to build up a straw man about those items for which he is only asking one-twelfth and those for which he is asking other fractions.
We understand perfectly the reason for that. He dealt with it very carefully and cleverly for new members in that rather professorial speech with which he began his morning's remarks. But I am glad, as are all members of the opposition, that we have smoked out the minister and that he is unable to provide us with this list of items which he

is not prepared to support. He said that in the short time that he was having lunch he was able to find these thirteen precedents-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say anything about lunch.

Oh, he did not have any lunch. For the benefit of new members he pointed out that these main estimates are actually prepared by the various departments of government in the early fall and cleared through treasury board generally in December. Then before the actual reference of the estimates to the house there are other things which arise which sometimes occasion the need for more money and sometimes occasion the need for less money. But when these estimates were presented by a government in good faith the government believed that all the money they asked for was needed and they stood behind that submission of estimates.
Naturally if, during the course of the year as the months rolled by it was found that some requirements were not going to be needed it was of course the proper action for a minister to take to stand up and inform the house, as did the Minister of Finance, apparently to the chagrin of the hon. member for Eglinton. He beat the hon. member for Eglinton to the punch and apparently the recollection of it still rankles. It is the proper function of the minister to inform the house that this money is not needed. But that is a very different course of conduct from what we saw on Tuesday when he announced to the house that he was at that time supporting only some of the estimates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his remark a few moments ago the Minister of Finance chose to criticize me for having suggested that the Prime Minister should have kept his election promise to call parliament in September to deal with the question of old age pensions. Let me make it clear that the Prime Minister made that promise not just once but on several occasions. He did it in a speech at Toronto on April 25. He repeated the promise in the city of Hull on May 7 and in Guelph, Ontario, on May 13. He gave the same promise again in a telecast over the C.B.C. on May 22 and in a C.B.C. radio talk from Vancouver on May 24. As a matter of fact, he made the promise in a speech as late as June 9, the day before the election, that if the Conservatives were returned to power they would call a September session of parliament to deal with the question of old age pensions.
The Minister of Finance suggested that that promise could not be fulfilled for two reasons, both of which he blames on the previous administration. He says, first of all, that the
Interim Supply
previous administration had made an arrangement a number of years ago for the universal postal union to meet in this chamber during the month of September. I remind hon. members opposite-and I call the Postmaster General as witness-that they knew of those arrangements. Those arrangements were debated in this House of Commons last March or April and I presume the Prime Minister was here. At least he should have known what was going on.
The present Postmaster General who then sat near us on this side of the house complained about those arrangements. The Conservatives knew that this building was committed for September to the universal postal union when the Prime Minister made this promise to call parliament in September. If he did not intend to carry out the promise because of that fact he should have said so or, having made the promise, he should have made other arrangements so far as the universal postal union was concerned.
The other excuse which the Minister of Finance now puts forth for the Prime Minister's not carrying out this promise-and this is the Prime Minister who on election night and several times since then said, "I will keep faith"-was the arrangement made by the previous government for Her Majesty to be here in mid-October. I am satisfied that the Prime Minister knew of this arrangement as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to give this house the reason why I think he must have known. Last April, shortly before we came to the end of the session, the former prime minister chose to call in spokesmen of groups on this side of the house in order to indicate what the plans were for the balance of that session. My leader happened to be ill at the time and when it was the turn of the spokesman for the C.C.F. to be called in, I was called to the office of the former prime minister. He told me-and I think he would not mind my saying this-that he had already spoken to the then leader of the opposition. I do not know what he told the then leader of the opposition but I know what he told me. He told me, amongst other things, of the plans for Her Majesty the Queen to come here in October. He also told me that the reason supply was being asked for to the end of October rather than to the end of September, as had been originally planned, was so that the opening of parliament, if it was so desired, could be delayed in order for Her Majesty to carry out that function.

Interim Supply
I do not know what the then prime minister told the then leader of the opposition but I would be greatly surprised if he told me, the second spokesman of a minority party, more than he told the then leader of the official opposition. I suggest that not only was there that private discussion-and I am sure that I am not breaking any confidence now in referring to it-but there were references in the house to the fact that Her Majesty the Queen was coming to the North American continent this fall. I am satisfied that the Prime Minister, when he was campaigning for the election and promising a September session of parliament, knew that Her Majesty was going to come here in October.
The Minister of Finance cannot get away with the display that he tried to indulge in and the suggestion that I would have robbed the Canadian people of the experience we have had this week because of the presence of Her Majesty. I recall to the Minister of Finance and repeat what I said this morning, namely that I think it would have been even more memorable and even more historic and would have given something even more lasting to the Canadian people if Her Majesty, on October 14, the day that she was here, had been given the opportunity, not just to open parliament and wonder what was coming but to give royal assent in person to a bill increasing the old age pension, a bill increasing the war veterans allowance and some of the other things that could have been passed by now if the Prime Minister had kept his sacred promise to call parliament in September. It is not good enough for the 5,000 senior citizens who die every month, the 5,000 or 10,000 who will never get whatever increase is in mind because the present government found a way to wiggle out of the promise it made.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Oh,
yes; to wiggle out, to renege on the sacred promise made to the people of this country, particularly to our senior citizens, who incidentally were singled out for particular notice by being mentioned first with regard to domestic matters in the speech from the throne. I say again that it would have been far more memorable if Her Majesty had been given this other opportunity.
This idea is not original with me. In the press comments as to what would happen after the new government took office some newspaper columnists suggested that this was a solution to the problem of what to do because Her Majesty was coming in October, namely that the session could be called in September as planned and arrangements
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
could be made for royal assent in person in October. I suggest that it would have been just as much for the pleasure of the Canadian people to have that happen as to have the interesting experience that we have had this week.
The Minister of Finance twits me for asking him for something which he says is unconstitutional or not in keeping with the rules of procedure. He says that I must not ask him in advance of resolutions being placed on the order paper, with the approval of the governor general, as to what the government proposes to bring down. The Minister of Justice will recall that last year or the year before he complained because the then prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, announced certain proposals regarding university grants and the Canada Council in advance of the speech from the throne. He complained that this was giving, before the governor general read the speech from the throne, information that should not be given until the speech from the throne was brought down.
Well, the Minister of Finance did the same thing this year. Toward the end of June or early in July he made a speech or gave a press release in which he announced that there would be a budget this fall and that there would be an increase in the old age pension. In other words, he committed the same sin which the Minister of Justice complained about when it was committed a year ago by the then prime minister.
I do not say that it is a sin to announce some of the intentions of the government, so long as the government makes it clear that it will merely recommend certain things to parliament but recognizes that parliament has the final word with regard to these matters.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if it was competent for him, in advance of the reading of the speech from the throne, to announce something which was going to be in the speech from the throne-that is to say, an increase in the amount of the old age pension-then it is competent for us to ask him for further details with respect to the matter. It was in that spirit that I sent him the telegram to which I referred and which I think should now be placed on the record: It is dated at Winnipeg July 2, 1957:
Hon. Donald Fleming,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Your announcement of an increase in old age pension this fall heartily welcomed by all. It would mean a great deal to our senior citizens if you would confirm now by further public announcement that the government will recommend that the pension be increased to not less than $60 a month in keeping with the figure mentioned by

Mr. Diefenbaker when he spoke In the House of Commons on March 28 this year. Retired federal civil servants also counting on early announcement of pension increases for those in lower and middle brackets in line with support to our demands for same given in past by prominent members of your party. Remember also Mr. Diefenbaker's support of our insistence on a substantial increase in basic $25 pension paid to C.N.R. employees. Trust announcement of action on this matter will be made soon. Please reply.
Stanley Knowles, Winnipeg North Centre.
As I say, I have to date received no reply to that telegram which was simply a request that the minister make more clear and more precise the details of an announcement which he had chosen to make, despite the fact that it was dealing with a matter which was to be included in the speech from the throne. As for chiding anyone on this side of the chamber for seeking information as to the intentions of the government, I suggest that no member on the other side who was in parliament before can do any such chiding and get away with it.
My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, tried time and time again when he was on this side of the chamber to get information out of the late government. Constitutional and procedural technicalities did not seem to bother him then. Now, all of a sudden constitutional and procedural technicalities seem to be something behind which he can hide because of his unwillingness to disclose this information. In that connection the motion which is before the committee of supply today asks us to continue for another month, the month of November, the expenditure programs of the old government, with a few changes involving the further supplementary estimates No. 2. I submit that a parliament which was told there was going to be a September session for dealing with old age pensions and was told that information would be given has the right to that information now. Are we going to have to wait, no one knows how long, until these changes are brought into being?
If the members on the government benches really believe in the supremacy of parliament and if they believe in the right of the members of parliament to be given information and not to be met with an iron curtain of secrecy, about which they used to complain,
I submit that they have no right to stand up and make speeches of the kind that was made today by the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to return for a moment to the question of the large number of unemployed and the increasing unemployment problem. In my own constituency at least seven or eight lumber mills have closed down throwing out of work some four or five hundred lumber workers.
Interim Supply
The Prime Minister in his pre-election promises indicated that he was prepared to increase the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Now while that is simply a palliative and it would not increase the market for lumber, I think in view of the rising cost of living something should be done in this regard and that it should not be left to the end of the session. Some action should be taken immediately.
I want to touch also upon the matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West. You will recall that I raised this question on the second day on which parliament convened. I asked the Prime Minister if he would be prepared to carry out his promise to consider the question of stock piling base metals and maintaining a floor price on those metals, that is to say, lead, zinc, copper and so on, metals which have depreciated in price to such an extent that many hard rock miners, particularly in western Canada, are being pressed to the wall. They too will, of course, be seeking unemployment insurance this winter and will be looking forward with very great interest to any increases that the Minister of Labour may be prepared to recommend. I was disappointed by the answer which I received from the right hon. Prime Minister and I hope that this is not another example of breaking faith with the people of Canada.
When the officers and other delegates of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers waited upon the Prime Minister and his cabinet there was undoubtedly a threat of increased tariffs on lead and zinc entering into the United States, but that was not the basis of their representations. The basis of their representations was that because of the price of metals at this moment, and at that moment in which they appeared which I believe was on August 6 last, many mines were being closed down. The large producers were curtailing production. As a matter of fact, in the paper-the Mine Mill Herald-which is distributed to its various members, they show pictures of deserted mining camps and ghost towns.
Now while the Prime Minister appeared to give very careful consideration to the delegation, it is quite obvious that he missed the point, and that is that prices are such at this moment that mines were being closed and miners are being thrown out of work. This was not something in anticipation of action by Congress of the United States. For that matter it is being discussed at this very moment.
I read in the paper while I was coming here on the train that the western metal mining interests had been granted another

Interim Supply
hearing on the question of the increased tariff against our metals, so that question was not the paramount one in my mind. The Prime Minister promised consideration of this matter, and I simply asked the Prime Minister if he was still giving consideration to the question; not to disclose the policy of the government, but to let us know that he is still giving continuous attention to the subject and not forgetting it, as he appears to have done judging from the answer he made to my question yesterday.
I cannot help but take a few minutes in which to congratulate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the very good work which they did during the visit of Her Majesty the Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh. There is no doubt that it was the finest effort on a large scale that has ever been carried out anywhere on the North American continent and I am indeed grateful that the result will remain on the record for all time and that it will be shown, undoubtedly, for many years to come. I am pleased that all Canada and all the western world will, no doubt, be able to see the pageantry that marked the occasion and the history that was made here during that visit. But there is one thing on which I am not quite clear. I have been unable to determine, despite my inquiries, just where the authority arose for the installation of television cameras in the Commons chamber for the purpose of telecasting the actual proceedings of the house. Much of the speech made yesterday by the Prime Minister had to do with the rights and the supremacy of parliament and the rights of members of parliament, and I am wondering how many members of parliament were contacted in order to determine whether they were prepared to accept this change in procedure. I know this sounds like a very small matter, but when the question of rights and privileges is being discussed in such glowing terms by members of the government I think it is appropriate that we should look into the whole question.
In 1954 the former leader of the Conservative party, the Hon. George Drew, took very great exception to the fact that a wire recorder was used experimentally in a committee-the committee on external affairs- and he had this to say in the House of Commons on a question of privilege. I will read part of what he said to show that he and many other members of his party felt that there should be no encroachment on the prerogatives of hon. members of this house. On page 3845 of Hansard of Wednesday, April 7, the Hon. George Drew said, and I quote in part:
I place this before you, Mr. Speaker, because there has been a very strong objection to the

Introduction of recording devices here in this house except in those cases whereby, with consent, the speeches of persons such as President Eisenhower or Mr. Churchill or others who recently visited us were broadcast.
Then he goes on to say:
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that is is not within the authority of any committee to depart from established practices in regard to methods of procedure even though the committees have full right to decide their own procedure within well established rules.
I go on, quoting from the hon. gentleman's remarks:
If the committee has the right to start taking tape recordings by microphones which could then in turn be broadcast, either in whole or in part, then the next step could easily be television.
I think it is a wonderful thing that the people across Canada should be enabled to see the opening of parliament and procedures in this house, but I do inquire with regard to the change in procedure that was made and the encroachment on members' prerogatives by the action that was taken. I do not know where this action originated; I have not been able to contact the former Speaker. Perhaps those in authority on our side of the house agreed with the arrangement; nevertheless, when members of the present government feel so strongly about the supremacy of parliament and the prerogatives of hon. members within this house I feel that they should at least have contacted the 260 or more members who were to be televised on that occasion.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few general remarks to make, more particularly on one or two of the items dealing with the Department of Agriculture. I understood the Minister of Finance to say during his statement that the passage of this motion for supply would not in any way prejudice our rights to have full discussion of agriculture or other estimates during this session. If that is right, and if the minister can assure me that we will have the privilege of discussing the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for 1957 and 1958 during this session I will expedite the matter by taking my seat at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I gave that assurance in the most explicit terms. There is not one item here which will not be before us again in committee of supply, and there will be the fullest opportunity for examining it. It is not a question of privilege; it is a question of hon. members' rights which are fully preserved by the undertaking I gave in time-honoured terms during the debate.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, then I will resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, the debate on supply provides hon. members of this house with an opportunity to draw the attention of the administration to problems or difficulties which exist within their part of the realm, and which affect the constituencies they represent here. I rise at this time only to point out that there are very serious difficulties and problems in the prairie region, problems which have reached disastrous proportions.
The ruinous policies of the former government are only too evident in our part of the country, and at the present time in the particular area from which I come 60 to 75 per cent of the agricultural producers have not been permitted to deliver even one bushel of the grain on their farms this year. As the result of "flooded" elevators and the inability to get box cars farmers are in a disastrous position.
I wish to say that the hopes of all agricultural producers rose very rapidly when they heard from the present administration that it was the intention of this government to see that those engaged in agriculture would be assured of their fair share of the national income.
They are watching this house very closely and waiting patiently to see that this promise is carried out in meeting the dire situation that exists at the present time. I do think, however, immediate action is necessary to prevent a further decline which might occur even within the next few weeks before the debate on the address on the speech from the throne is completed and legislation is put through. I rise at this time because I firmly believe immediate action is necessary.
Agricultural producers in that area who are unable to deliver any grain have undertaken the arduous task of feeding much of that grain to livestock. Much of that livestock in the form of hogs is ready to market and cattle now constitute practically the only means by which they can receive remuneration for their year's work. The price to the producers of that livestock is dropping rapidly and they fear that a continuation of this trend will produce disastrous results.
I urge this as an immediate course of action on the part of the present administration and I direct my remarks particularly to the Minister of Agriculture because the people in that area are looking to him for action. In order to prevent a decline we urge that two steps be taken. The first is that an immediate floor price be established on all livestock products. Already the prices of these commodities on the market are below the costs of production. Should a further decline
Interim Supply
occur it cannot fail to have disastrous consequences. At this time of year particularly on the regular market operations a decline seems to be inevitable.
The second step we would urge the minister to adopt, if necessary by order in council, is that he immediately set up a board of livestock commissioners to ensure that livestock, and particularly cattle as it is taken from the producer, is properly graded. At the present time there is no proper grading of livestock to protect the interest of the producer. When he brings his livestock to the stockyard he has to accept whatever grade and price the packing house buyers offer him for his commodity. It then goes on the market and he has no assurance that his animals are graded properly and must accept whatever price and grade they see fit to place upon it.
I outline these two steps as a matter of deep concern and as a course of action which will do a great deal to restore confidence in the hearts and minds of Canadian agricultural producers that this government intends to see that this important segment of our population receives a fair share of the national income. I do not believe these producers can be assured of their share of the national income unless these two steps are taken. I sincerely urge the government to do this now in order to prevent a further decline and increased suffering on the part of those who are looking to this government for some remedy for this grave situation. I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance and seriousness of this question and it would be a matter of extremely wise policy on the part of the government to immediately carry out the two steps I have indicated.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak on this motion because I have been endeavouring to find out something concerning the promise of an amount of money that was to be made available for extra work on the Canadian National Railways in Moncton and at other terminal points.
On July 10, 1957, His Worship M. M. Baig, mayor of Moncton, Hon. Joseph Bourgeois, minister without portfolio in the New Brunswick government and I sent a telegram to nine of the cabinet ministers of the present government in which we protested the layoff in the shops, asked reconsideration of the matter and recommended the building of additional railway equipment in Moncton. This was not a strange request at all because a few years ago the present Minister of Transport came to Moncton as the president of the

Interim Supply
Progressive Conservative association and at that time termed the existing layoff as deplorable and unnecesary.
However, when I ask him about the same matter now he does not give the same answer. Instead, when I ask him about layoffs although he still continues to say he considers them deplorable he brushes off the subject very quickly and advises that layoffs have to take place from time to time. Apparently now he believes that layoffs have to take place from time to time on the C.N.R. in Moncton and at other points and although I agree with him that this is true under the present circumstances I contend, as he did, that they would be unnecessary if more equipment was built and repaired at the Moncton shops, especially dining car equipment which used to be repaired and built there. There would then be more employment available and these men would not have to be laid off.
When a proposed layoff in the C.N.R. was suggested some two or three years ago the present Minister of Transport as president of the Progressive Conservative association was reported in the press as offering an explanation for the layoffs in these words:
Mr. Hees charged that the situation created by shops lay-offs in this area was aggravated because the work was being shifted to Montreal where the additional employment would mean little, if anything, to that city.
Apparently there is lots of work available in Montreal. The press report continues:
''But," he said, "it is a very serious blow to the Moncton area."
If that was the policy of his party at that time, and he was speaking as president of the Progressive Conservative association, it should be his policy today as Minister of Transport and that of his party.
In answer to our telegram and to the many others addressed to the minister on the same subject we were advised that money would be made available to the Canadian National Railways for the purpose of carrying out extra work in the C.N.R. shops. When I left Moncton a short time ago the men who had been laid off were still not working. The minister advises that the offer is still open to the C.N.R. to institute such a program but apparently that is where his sense of responsibility toward these men who are now walking the streets of Moncton ends. Incidentally some of them told me they voted for the Progressive Conservative party.
What I and the people of my constituency and people in other C.N.R. points as well want to know is how much money has been set aside by this government for extra work at the C.N.R. shops in Moncton and how

much has been set aside for additional work at other points on the C.N.R.? I want to know if this situation is going to be corrected or if that is as far as the minister intends to go.
The minister made an interesting statement which is reported in the August 21 issue of the Moncton Times. He said:
"As far as the federal government Is concerned, X feel we have done our part."
I do not for one moment believe that the federal government has done its part and it will not have done it until these men are again working in the C.N.R. shops. As the minister said on a previous occasion, the layoff is unnecessary and deplorable and should be remedied by the creation of additional employment in the Moncton shops.
He told us before that the layoff was caused by work being shifted to Montreal. I want to know whether that has any effect on the present layoff. Is that what is happening now? Is work being shifted to Montreal? Besides those men who are laid off from the Canadian National Railways, which is making our unemployment situation worse and worse because there are twice as many people unemployed in the province of New Brunswick now as there were a year ago, there are the former employees of the Canadian government railways and C.N.R. who are on very small pensions.
On May 6, 1957, the former leader of the opposition visited Moncton. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Moncton Times in which the present Prime Minister promised a reconsideration of the Canadian National Railway pension schemes which he claimed were "totally inadequate". The Minister of Transport, in an answer to my question concerning these pensions, gave me the old "due course" answer; when there was anything to announce that he would do it in due course. Well there are not too many pensioners of the old government railway in Moncton; there are several Canadian National Railways pensioners and in due course they are all going to die. I want to know from the minister what action is going to be taken to assist these aged pensioners of the C.N.R., and whether he believes, as his leader does, that these pensions are wholly inadequate.
I have taken up this time to put this on the record because I find there is a great deal to be learned from new cabinet ministers. They are not the same people that they were when they were private members sitting on this side of the house. They are now very concerned with following the rules and that questions must go on the order paper. They disregard your questions by suggesting that

you put them on the order paper. This is a practice that I can well remember was not carried out by the new Minister of Transport when he was a private member.
These matters concern money and the voting of money and I would like the answers some time before this motion is passed. How much money has been allotted to the Canadian National Railways for extra work at C.N.R. points? What is the authority for granting this money? I should like also to know how much money has been set aside to look after these-to use the words of the Prime Minister-wholly inadequate pensions of the former Canadian National Railways employees? I know the minister will not repudiate his statement of 1954 and I urge that answers be given and that he tell us what is being done to assist these men in Moncton and in other centres.

Mr. Chairman, there is a matter which I wish to raise at this time. It has considerable urgency or else I would not be taking up the time of the committee in raising it. It is also a very practical matter. I assure the committee that there will be no sound and fury connected with this. It is a modest request which I think the Minister of Finance will appreciate very well, and which I am sure his colleagues will be willing to go along with at the earliest possible opportunity.
Hon. members will recall in previous sessions the question of aid to municipalities, so far as this parliament grants aid, has been brought up on a number of occasions. One particular field in which this government could help many municipalities at this time would be in making available funds for capital outlay which today is costing the average municipality a large amount of money. I think it is commonly known that the issuing of debentures for capital expenditures is becoming more and more expensive. Because of the increase in the cost of such debentures and the discounts which the municipalities have to offer at this time the problem is becoming of very serious concern to municipalities right across the country.
The former member for Okanagan Boundary on many occasions raised the question of reactivating, or making use of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, which was placed on the statutes in 1938 and which has a provision under which the Minister of Finance, with the consent of the government, may advance moneys to municipalities at 2 per cent for self-liquidating projects. We know that this act has not been used for a number of years. The standard reply, whenever the hon. member, and others to whom I
Interim Supply
shall refer in a moment, asked the government to put the provisions of this act back into practice was that this was designed primarily as a relief measure during the days of unemployment, and that it was not considered desirable to use the act in recent years.
From that point of view alone, considering the speech we have just heard from the hon. member for Westmorland, and from hon. members who have spoken in the last day or two, it would appear that the situation now calls for a re-appraisal of this act. Perhaps the unemployment situation alone would warrant the use of this act, but there is a more important reason than merely the unemployment situation, namely the financial position in which the municipalities find themselves.
I do not need to weary the committee with many statistics. All we need to do is to look through the accounts of the municipalities of Canada and we shall find that they are going into debt. Not only that, they are finding it increasingly difficult, even at an enhanced interest rate, to sell their debentures unless they offer them at a considerable discount. The result of that is that many very desirable projects either are being postponed or delayed by the municipalities because of the cost of money during these inflationary times. The cost of materials and labour is high. The cost of raising capital, in addition to other costs, is becoming prohibitive. If the government were to reactivate this act, put it into effect and make use of it, I feel sure that they could make a very substantial saving for the municipalities right across this country.
I have hope that the government will do this because looking back through the record I find that not only did the former member for Okanagan Boundary champion this cause in the house very ably but to his assistance came various other members of the opposition, including the then official opposition. The hon. member for Greenwood spoke on this question as late as the 21st of February of this year and in order to show how strongly the Progressive Conservative party was behind the idea of granting some assistance to municipalities he put on the record an amendment that had been moved by the former leader of the Progressive Conservative party, Mr. Drew, on April 30, 1956. I should like to quote that part of the amendment dealing with the question of aid to municipalities. It can be found at page 1510 of Hansard of February 21, 1957 and is in these words: This house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to measures to assist the municipalities of Canada to meet their mounting financial problems . . .
That is not the end of the amendment but I stop there because that is the part having

Interim Supply
to do with the matter I am now discussing. I draw to the attention of the government the fact that that amendment was moved on April 30, 1956, and the speeches which followed indicated that the problem was immediate and urgent at that time. A considerable length of time, approximately a year and a half, has elapsed and the problem has become more urgent and more immediate. I think that the government should now be prepared to make use of that act to help to alleviate the situation.
I should also like to mention that later the same day the hon. member for Vancouver East made a very strong plea for the use of this legislation in order to help municipalities to obtain capital funds at a reasonable cost. Referring again to the record, we find that on the 21st of February the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary once more made his plea, and as we go through the record we find that even as late as March of this year all three parties then in opposition were advocating strongly that the act should be used for that purpose. I do not wish to take the time to find the references but members of the Social Credit party also took the same position.
In view of what had taken place I wrote to the Minister of Finance about this matter on September 30 this year and in that letter I brought to his attention by way of reminder the demands that had been made by the three parties in opposition which, incidentally, now control a majority of the house and are in a position to carry out the things which they advocate. I asked him if he would be prepared to recommend to the government at the earliest possible opportunity that the act be put back into operation. I received a reply from the minister on the 5th of October, and I will only quote that part of the letter having to do with this matter. It is in these words:
I have carefully noted your suggestions concerning the revived use of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. This subject has been given some consideration. I know that you realize that the concurrence of the provincial government in each case is required with respect to every project under the terms of that legislation.
That is the end of the letter so far as this question is concerned. I am going to make particular reference to the last part of the minister's reply where he points out that in each case the concurrence of the province is required with regard to funds advanced for a particular project because I would not want the committee or the public to get the impression that the concurrence of the provincial government is required for the purpose of putting the act back into business. That is not the case.
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
All that is required is an order in council by the government. The matter does not even require parliamentary action. The act is now on the statute books. It has been there since 1938 and is still valid legislation. All that would be required would be for the government to pass an order in council proclaiming that the act is available to municipalities requiring such funds. It is only if any municipality then applied for a loan under the act that the provincial government would come into the picture. The way that the government of the province comes into the picture is simply that they have to guarantee to the federal government the loan advanced to the municipality, something which in the natural course of events I feel sure any provincial government would do.
In fact some provincial governments are now doing something similar to what is provided in this act without any participation by the federal government at all. They are doing it on their own. It would be very much easier for them simply to have to guarantee such loans than actually to have to advance the money involved.
That being the case and considering the history of the demands made by the members of the parties then in the opposition I would expect that with the least possible delay and at a very early date the federal government would make such an announcement. If they feel that they would like to consult with the provinces before doing so, I see nothing wrong with that. In fact, that is one reason why I am raising the question at this time. We know that in a reasonably short time there will be a dominion-provincial conference at which this and other related matters will be discussed. That would be a most appropriate and convenient time for the federal government to consult with the provincial premiers as to their readiness to participate in the operation of the act if the federal government should decide to put it into effect.
I do wish to make an earnest plea to the government not to forget the provisions of this act and I do so because of the plight in which municipalities find themselves. I suppose examples could be given by any member of the house. I refer only to those that concern my own constituency, and I happen to know that there are municipalities in my constituency which are finding it very difficult to sell debentures at the interest rate to which they have been accustomed traditionally, and even at the higher interest rate at which such debentures are now being offered they are finding that they have to sell them at a considerable discount.
This means that there is a totally unnecessary drain upon the taxpayers of the particular municipality in providing funds which

are available under federal legislation which the government of recent years has not seen fit to use, but which I hope the present government will be prepared to make use of in view of the attitude they took even as late as February and March of this year.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising to say a word or two about the further supplementary estimates, No. 2, the part of the estimates for which I imagine the Minister of Finance takes full responsibility along with his other colleagues even though he seems, in a singular display of lack of collective responsibility, to have dissociated himself from his other colleagues with respect to the earlier estimates. However, my hon. friend, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, smoked out from the Minister of Finance an admission which we were all interested and, I think, surprised to hear, that after four months in office he had not yet been able to find any savings he could make in the estimates we brought before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said no such thing.
And he hoped that by trying hard for the next six months he would be able to find something somewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Are you preaching for a call too?
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That bears no resemblance whatever to what I said.
I am not preaching for a call nor am I preaching. I leave that to the Prime Minister. I, sir, have no pretensions of being a Billy Sunday or even a Billy Graham.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There is another form of "Billy" though.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You certainly do not have the qualifications.

Nor do I pretend to have them. When hon. gentlemen opposite have finished their jeering, perhaps I can, following the example that the Prime Minister gave us yesterday, continue with my remarks, which are serious. When Mr. Harris was minister of finance I was able to persuade him to put into the estimates a sum of some $40 million for the department for which I then had responsibility.
I observe that far from finding any savings to make in that department, the new government has increased the estimates of that department-and has done it entirely on its own responsibility-by practically another $10 million which is a 25 per cent increase. That 96698-7
Interim Supply
is, I suppose, as big an increase as there has ever been in the estimates of a peacetime department since confederation.
I had lunch, unlike the Minister of Finance, and therefore I was not able to look up any phony precedents. But I should be greatly surprised if halfway through a year, the estimates of a civil department in peacetime ever before had to be increased by 25 per cent. No doubt that was because Mr. Harris was so very thrifty and I was so very willing to go along with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It might be bad estimating.

It was not bad estimating on the high side, as I think the acting minister will be obliged to admit, because he must take the responsibility for asking for this amount of money, namely nearly $10 million. I would not be greatly surprised if the minister asked for more and, like Oliver Twist, got treated by the Minister of Finance in the way in which Oliver Twist was treated, this Minister of Finance who is trying to give the public the impression that he is the same kind of overseer as there was in Oliver Twist, but who is not making much of a job of it.
I should not be at all surprised if the Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, for whose abilities I must confess I have more respect than I have for those of most of the other occupants of the treasury benches and for whose abilities the Prime Minister evidently has more respect than he has for those of most of his colleagues because he has given him two extremely heavy portfolios to carry, has good and adequate reasons for all these increases.
I am not rising with any suggestion that they should be opposed, at least until I have heard the explanation of them. I am rising for another reason. A good deal has been said since the election about the subject of immigration and something was said about it before the election. What was said before the election, by hon. gentlemen opposite, is so different from the things they have been saying since the election that I feel that before this large sum of money is voted we should be given some kind of explanation of this light which they saw, not on the road to Damascus but on the road to office, which seems to have changed so completely the kind of opinions they expressed before the election.
The Prime Minister made a speech to an organization which we all know and which I certainly respect greatly. This organization has done a great deal to help in making better Canadians of the newcomers who have come to our country to become citizens. I refer to the Ethnic Press Association. The Prime Minister made a speech to them which is

Interim. Supply
reported in the Globe and Mail which at that time was an almost slavish organ of hon. gentlemen opposite. I understand the Globe and Mail now sometimes criticize them but at that time it did not do so. I would presume that the Prime Minister and his colleagues would be quite satisfied with the Globe and Mail report. It appeared on April 27 of this year and states as follows:
At his first stop of the day-
That refers to the present Prime Minister. -a conference with the Ethnic Press Association in Toronto-Mr. Diefenbaker filled in the detail of one aspect of that program.
I may say that the previous part of the report refers to his program generally.
Development, he told the editors of foreign language publications, demands manpower. The only way to meet the needs for skill and talents is through accelerated-
And I emphasize that word "accelerated". -immigration.
Mind you, this was in April of this year.
A government formed by the Conservatives, he added, will undertake an intensive immigration policy that will make available to all sections of the country those talents and skills.
The Conservatives, he continued, will end the arbitrary and unjust interpretation of immigration regulations which have been a feature of Liberal immigration policy and which have constituted a denial and vote of immigration legislation.
I think there must be a misprint of some kind there.
The only limit on immigration-
And this is the part I should particularly like to draw to the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite.
__should be the capacity of Canada to absorb
newcomers into her economic life.
That, I may say, is straight Liberal doctrine taken from Mr. Mackenzie King's statement in this house on May 1, 1947, a statement about immigration policy that has worn very well and one that I think the present government will find it fairly hard to depart from without getting themselves into serious trouble.
Australia's forward-looking immigration policy,-
In those days the Prime Minister was perhaps a greater admirer of Australia than he was after he came back from London.
__Mr. Diefenbaker emphasized, has produced the
conclusion that it can absorb just under four per cent a year of its total population.
Such a yardstick applied to Canada would establish the target of 640,000 immigrants a year, or more than four times the number that came to Canada in 1956.
I leave hon. members to form their own estimate as to why this speech was made to the Ethnic Press Association instead of, for example, being made to the Loyal Orange

Association. However, it was a fairly definite statement that the Prime Minister intended to increase immigration by two or three times what we were achieving in the year 1957, which is, or will turn out to have been, the greatest year for immigration since 1913. Of course I regard the figure of 640,000 as being a completely fantastic figure for any one year. However that is the figure the Prime Minister used, presumably when he was appealing to the people to vote for him to carry out his policies, and presumably he meant what he said. Of course, if he did not mean what he said, those of us on this side of the house would think that he should not have said it.
But what do we find? The first thing this government did, the very first action they took to change anything after they came into office, was to restrict the existing immigration. Far from accelerating it or intensifying it, they restricted it severely and handled it in such a ham-handed fashion, if I may use that expression, that the officials of the department for days afterwards were obliged to explain what the minister had meant by the original statement he issued.
Those of us who have had some experience in this field know that after the efforts that had been made by Mr. Harris, myself and the officials of the department under our direction for a good many years to build up a service in the United Kingdom, we were really getting a response this year and were getting the best class of immigrants that we have obtained for years from the United Kingdom. This whole movement had cold water poured on it by the hon. gentleman who was giving his spare time to the immigration department while he was learning how to be Minister of Justice evidently because his colleague the hon. member for Three Rivers was not considered to be worthy of occupying the post of Minister of Justice.
Oh, oh.
There may be another explanation, but that is one the press gave.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Pretty mean!

In any event, whatever the reason the Prime Minister may have had for giving no departmental responsibilities to the hon. member for Three Rivers, the hon. member for St. John's West or the hon. member for Greenwood and giving two portfolios to the hon. member for Kamloops, I do not know it.
And you will probably never find out.

Perhaps, but I do know that there are probably very few members on either side of the house who will accuse me

of being indolent in the performance of my duties when I occupied the office of Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

Not indolent but
ineffective.

Well, of course, I think the proof of the pudding is probably in the eating. Yes, I was ineffective. I was ineffective because I encouraged immigration, but the hon. gentleman is effective, yes, in stopping it.
Now it has always been the policy of the Liberal party, and it still is our policy, that we should not encourage people to come to this country to be unemployed. I would not for a moment advocate an immigration policy which was going to bring more people into Canada than could be absorbed and be absorbed fairly readily and quickly into the economy. That was our policy and it was one which proved pretty successful over the past 10 years when we had a greater growth in our population than in any previous period in our history. It may be that it was wise in all the circumstances to give careful consideration-as I had planned to give had I remained in office-to what should be the course to be taken later in the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You had already decided to restrict immigration and issued instructions on April 12.
That statement, Mr. Chairman, is not in any proper sense of the word correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is absolutely correct and I have the departmental papers in front of me to prove it.

I may say that I did ask the officials of the department to make a very careful study of what should be done after the election. I made no final decision except with respect to certain arrangements that had been made with regard to transportation and certain other technical arrangements which it had begun to appear to me would not be necessary. I did consider, however, that later in the year-and this has happened of course every year-it would be desirable to discourage persons coming into Canada to seek employment. It has been our experience in every year but one since the war that it was not wise to encourage people who were coming here to look for employment to come in the later months of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

Certainly.
